title: Mixture-of-Recursions: Learning Dynamic Recursive Depths for Adaptive Token-Level Computation
relevance_reason: Weight-tied recursive Transformer pretrained from scratch with learned token-level routers that set per-token recursion depth.
one_sentence: MoR adds MoD-style routers to a Middle-Cycle recursive Transformer so each token gets 1..Nr recursions; at equal training FLOPs it beats vanilla and fixed-depth recursive baselines (135M-1.7B) with fewer parameters and higher measured decode throughput.
key_contributions: Expert-choice (per-step top-k with hierarchical filtering, capacity fixed to Nr/Nr..1/Nr) and token-choice (one-shot top-1 depth assignment with balancing loss) routers trained from scratch inside a weight-tied recursion block.
Recursion-wise KV caching (only active tokens cache KV at each depth) and a recursive KV sharing variant (reuse first-recursion KV).
IsoFLOP and fixed-token comparisons at 135M-1.7B, plus throughput measured with continuous depth-wise batching.

setup.model_sizes: 135M, 360M, 730M, 1.7B base (vanilla) sizes; MoR/recursive have roughly 1/Nr unique parameters (e.g. 118M non-embedding at Nr=3 for the 360M base)
setup.train_tokens_or_data: FineWeb-Edu (SmolLM-Corpus subset); main table at 16.5e18 FLOPs or 20B tokens; isoFLOP budgets 2e18, 5e18, 16.5e18
setup.loops_train: Nr = 2, 3, 4 (max recursions); Middle-Cycle sharing with unique first and last layers
setup.loops_test: same Nr as training; per-token depth 1..Nr set by router
setup.baselines: Vanilla Transformer (Llama-style, SmolLM configs); fixed-depth Recursive Transformer with same sharing
setup.benchmarks: FineWeb-Edu validation NLL; LAMBADA, HellaSwag, PIQA, WinoGrande, ARC, MMLU few-shot; decode throughput on H100

claims.claim: At equal training FLOPs, MoR (expert-choice, Nr=2) beats the vanilla Transformer in average few-shot accuracy with about half the parameters, because routing lets it process more tokens in the same budget.
claims.regime: iso_train_flop (not iso_param: MoR has ~50% fewer parameters; not iso_data: MoR sees more tokens)
claims.evidence_quote: the MoR model, using an expert-choice router and two recursions, achieves a lower validation loss and surpasses the vanilla baseline in average few-shot accuracy (43.1% vs. 42.3%).

claims.claim: At equal training tokens (20B), MoR Nr=2 beats vanilla and fixed-depth recursive with 25% fewer training FLOPs and measured 19% less training time and 25% lower peak memory.
claims.evidence_quote: our model reduces training time by 19% and cuts peak memory usage by 25%.

claims.claim: In isoFLOP sweeps MoR beats fixed-depth recursive at every size but underperforms vanilla at 135M; it matches or exceeds vanilla only above 360M.
claims.evidence_quote: While it underperforms the vanilla model at the smallest model size (135M)—likely due to a recursive capacity bottleneck—this gap closes rapidly at scale.

claims.claim: Expert-choice routing outperforms token-choice routing at Nr=3; token-choice struggles with load balancing for a long initial phase of training.
claims.evidence_quote: using token-choice routing yields lower performance (40.0%) compared to expert-choice routing (42.6%), indicating that routing granularity plays a pivotal role in model performance.

claims.claim: Measured decode throughput with continuous depth-wise batching exceeds vanilla for all MoR variants, up to 2.06x for MoR-4 at max batch size, with slight quality loss; the timing excludes KV cache update cost.
claims.regime: unclear (throughput at fixed or memory-maximal batch; models trained at equal FLOPs)
claims.evidence_quote: Increasing recursion depth leads to more tokens exiting early and a further reduction in KV cache usage. This, in turn, boosts throughput significantly (e.g., MoR-4 achieves up to a 2.06× speedup with 𝐵 = Max).

claims.claim: With the auxiliary loss, router scores for selected vs unselected tokens are almost perfectly separated, so the top-k capacity cannot be changed after training (no inference-time budget control).
claims.evidence_quote: the router outputs for selected and unselected tokens are almost perfectly separated. This makes it challenging to adjust top-k values after training.

numbers.what: Avg few-shot accuracy, MoR (expert, Nr=2) vs vanilla at 16.5e18 training FLOPs
numbers.quote: achieves a lower validation loss and surpasses the vanilla baseline in average few-shot accuracy (43.1% vs. 42.3%). Remarkably, this superior performance is achieved despite using nearly 50% fewer parameters.

numbers.what: Training FLOP reduction of MoR Nr=2 vs vanilla at 20B tokens
numbers.quote: our MoR model with 𝑁𝑟 = 2 outperforms both vanilla and recursive baselines—achieving lower validation loss and higher accuracy—despite using 25% fewer training FLOPs.

numbers.what: Measured training time and peak memory reduction vs vanilla (20B tokens)
numbers.quote: This theoretical efficiency translates into significant practical gains: compared to the vanilla baseline, our model reduces training time by 19% and cuts peak memory usage by 25%.

numbers.what: Max decode throughput speedup MoR-4 vs vanilla (360M, B=Max)
numbers.quote: This, in turn, boosts throughput significantly (e.g., MoR-4 achieves up to a 2.06× speedup with 𝐵 = Max).

numbers.what: Token-choice vs expert-choice avg few-shot accuracy at Nr=3
numbers.quote: using token-choice routing yields lower performance (40.0%) compared to expert-choice routing (42.6%), indicating that routing granularity plays a pivotal role

numbers.what: KV memory and IO of recursion-wise caching relative to vanilla
numbers.quote: Recursion-wise caching cuts KV memory and IO to approximately (𝑁𝑟 + 1)/2𝑁𝑟 times across the entire model (when assuming capacity factors follow a sequence like 𝑁𝑟 /𝑁𝑟 , · · · , 1/𝑁𝑟 over 𝑁𝑟 recursion steps).

numbers.what: Expert-choice capacity schedule for Nr=3
numbers.quote: For example, when 𝑁𝑟 = 3, recursion steps 1, 2, and 3 handle {3/3, 2/3, 1/3} of tokens, respectively.

numbers.what: Max batch sizes under H100 memory (vanilla base 32)
numbers.quote: Under these adaptive conditions, MoR-2 supports a batch size of 42, MoR-3 supports 48, and MoR-4 supports up to 51.

numbers.what: Worst-case dead-token ratio of auxiliary-router variants (positional bias)
numbers.quote: some auxiliary router variants exhibit dead token ratios as high as 66.7%, suggesting that the router always selects tokens from the same positions across inputs, reflecting a positional bias.

numbers.what: Iso-param recursion scaling at 118M, 10B tokens: avg few-shot Nr=1 vs Nr=2

limitations: Up to 1.7B only; expert-choice capacity is fixed by hand (Nr/Nr..1/Nr), so the average depth is a hyperparameter, not learned, and cannot be changed after training because router scores saturate; token-choice suffers load imbalance for much of training; throughput timing excludes KV cache update cost; underperforms vanilla at 135M; no reasoning post-training studied.
survey_notes: Anchor paper for token-level routing. Key caveat for the loop-count section: in the main (expert-choice) configuration the fraction of tokens at each depth is a fixed capacity schedule chosen to mimic perfectly balanced token-choice, so MoR learns WHICH tokens go deep, not HOW MUCH compute to spend; savings are therefore set by design (KV memory (Nr+1)/2Nr) and the comparison is iso-training-FLOP with fewer parameters, not iso-param. Throughput gains (up to 2.06x) are measured wall-clock but rely on continuous depth-wise batching, larger max batch from smaller KV/params, and exclude KV update time. Failure modes reported: positional bias / dead tokens with auxiliary router, load imbalance with token-choice, saturated router scores preventing post-hoc budget change (this motivates budget-conditioned/elastic methods such as LoopFormer 2602.11451 and T-LoopFormer 2609.15160). Contrast with training-free convergence halting (see 2607.14427, 2603.08391 in this group), which needs no router but yields no training-time FLOP savings. Not iso-param vs vanilla: MoR wins partly by seeing more tokens.

title: Adaptive Loops and Memory in Transformers: Think Harder or Know More?
relevance_reason: Per-layer looping with a PonderNet-style learned halting router, compared to iso-param and iso-FLOP (3x deeper) baselines.
one_sentence: Each of 12 layers loops up to Nmax times with a PonderNet-style halting router (weighted mixture of iterates, no ponder penalty); looping helps math BPB even vs a 36-layer iso-FLOP model, while memory banks recover commonsense.
key_contributions: Per-layer adaptive looping: halting router on [h; t/Nmax], output is the halting-probability-weighted sum of iterates, softplus loop scales initialized near identity.
Gated local and global learned memory banks added to the looped model.
Analysis of learned expected loop count per layer: later layers loop more, and loop usage switches on at a consistent validation CE.

setup.model_sizes: ~200M, 12 layers (D=768); iso-FLOP baseline 36 layers (332M)
setup.train_tokens_or_data: FineWeb-Edu, ~14B tokens
setup.loops_train: Nmax in {3, 5, 7} per layer
setup.loops_test: same Nmax; output is weighted combination over all iterations
setup.baselines: Base 12-layer; iso-parameter wider-FFN model; iso-FLOP 36-layer model; memory variants
setup.benchmarks: OLMES commonsense (accuracy and BPB) and MATH subcategories (BPB only)

claims.claim: Adaptive looping (Nmax=3) reduces math BPB by 22% vs the base model and beats a 36-layer iso-FLOP model on math BPB by 6.4% with one-third of the layers.
claims.regime: iso_param (vs base/IsoPar) and iso_effective_depth/approx iso-FLOP at max loops (vs 36-layer, which has more parameters)
claims.evidence_quote: Intriguingly the improvement on math benchmarks remains when we compare against the IsoFLOP model (1.687 vs. 1.801, a 6.4% advantage) despite only having one-third the number of layers.

claims.claim: More loops add little beyond Nmax=3 (Loop-7 improves 1.7% over Loop-3) and commonsense slightly declines with more loops; the 36-layer iso-FLOP model remains better on commonsense.
claims.evidence_quote: When we further increase the number of loops, the performance increase is modest relative to the initial improvement from the base model (Loop-7 improves by 1.7% over Loop-3). Interestingly, commonsense performance shows a slight downward trend with more loops.

claims.claim: With no ponder penalty, the halting router learns layer-specialized depth: early layers loop minimally, later layers loop more; loop use starts only after validation CE falls to about 3.27.
claims.evidence_quote: The onset of the increase in the number of loops occurs at approximately the same validation cross-entropy value across all loop configurations, around 3.27 ± 0.59

claims.claim: The ponder penalty weight lambda is set to 0, so loop-count patterns are driven only by the LM loss; the paper does not measure compute savings from halting.
claims.evidence_quote: We set λ = 0 for the majority of our experiments, meaning the model receives no explicit incentive to minimize loop iterations.

numbers.what: Math BPB, adaptive Loop-3 vs base model
numbers.quote: Introducing adaptive looping with Nmax = 3 yields improvements in math BPB (1.687 vs. 2.163 for the base model, a 22% reduction) alongside moderate gains in commonsense accuracy (0.501 vs. 0.477)

numbers.what: Math BPB, Loop-3 vs 36-layer iso-FLOP
numbers.quote: the improvement on math benchmarks remains when we compare against the IsoFLOP model (1.687 vs. 1.801, a 6.4% advantage)

numbers.what: Model scale and data
numbers.quote: First, our experiments are at a relatively small scale (∼200M parameters, 12 layers, 14B tokens).

numbers.what: Memory gains over Loop-3
numbers.quote: Compared to our Loop-3 model without memory we further improve on math benchmarks by 4.2% and on commonsense accuracy by 2%

numbers.what: Loop scale initialization
numbers.quote: αt is initialized to −7.0, which ensures the loop begins as an approximate identity mapping, and the model gradually learns when and how much to intervene.

limitations: Small scale (~200M, 14B tokens); math measured by BPB not accuracy; no full compute-tradeoff characterization; halting is a soft weighted mixture over all Nmax iterations with lambda=0, so no inference savings are measured or claimed.
venue: Published at Latent & Implicit Thinking Workshop @ ICLR 2026
survey_notes: Learned-halting example where the halting distribution is used as a soft read-out (weighted mixture over iterates) rather than to save compute: all Nmax iterations are computed and no savings are reported. Useful for the 'what does a halting gate learn without a cost term' question: with lambda=0 the router does not collapse to max depth everywhere; it learns layer-specific depth (early layers ~1 step). The 36-layer iso-FLOP baseline has more parameters (332M vs 200M), so the math win is at matched effective depth but not matched parameters; commonsense loses to it, consistent with the knowledge-vs-manipulation split attributed to Ouro (2510.25741). Workshop paper, ~200M only.

title: Improving Test-Time Scaling with Adaptive Looped Transformers
relevance_reason: Post-trained full-stack looped LLM with a token-level learned iteration decider; compares fixed vs adaptive looping at matched decoding FLOPs.
one_sentence: Shows post-trained looped LLMs (Ouro/Huginn style) have steeper accuracy-vs-decode-FLOP slopes but lose to a non-looped baseline at matched compute; TaH2 jointly trains backbone and a per-token continue decider with online loss-gain labels and wins at matched compute.
key_contributions: Test-time scaling audit: slope of accuracy per doubling of decoding FLOPs for Standard, fixed/adaptive Ouro and Huginn post-trained from the same Qwen3 checkpoint and data.

Lookahead depth supervision: online continue labels from measured next-iteration loss reduction (coverage rho=0.99), cost-sensitive BCE decider loss, on-policy deterministic depth during training, stopping-weighted output mixture.
Depth-batched serving (extended Mini-SGLang) reporting real latency and throughput, not only FLOPs.

setup.model_sizes: Qwen3-1.7B, 4B, 8B Base backbones; updater and decider add <3% parameters
setup.train_tokens_or_data: 273K prompts (AM-Qwen3-Distilled + Nemotron-Agentic-v1), 3 epochs, 16K context, 3.4B tokens at 1.7B; 2 tokens per parameter for 4B/8B
setup.loops_train: depth ceiling M = 2, 4, 8 (full L-layer passes); Huginn baseline M = 3, 7 over 14 of 28 layers
setup.loops_test: same ceiling, adaptive per token with exit threshold 0.5; M=8 checkpoint also tested at ceilings 4 and 12
setup.baselines: Standard (M=1), TaH2-fixed, Ouro-style (fixed and exit-gate), Huginn-style, all post-trained from the same Qwen3 checkpoint with the same recipe
setup.benchmarks: AIME24-26, AMC23, MATH500, OlympiadBench, IMO-AnswerBench, GPQA, SuperGPQA, HumanEval, MBPP, LiveCodeBench v6, BFCL v3

claims.claim: Post-trained looped models (fixed Ouro, adaptive Ouro, Huginn) have steeper accuracy-compute slopes than the non-looped baseline yet are less accurate over the overlapping compute range.
claims.regime: iso_data, same checkpoint (iso_param backbone), compared at matched decoding FLOPs
claims.evidence_quote: Yet all three remain less accurate than Standard over the overlapping compute range; the exit gate lowers Ouro's decoding cost but does not close the gap.

claims.claim: Fixed-depth looping wastes compute: many tokens gain little or get worse from extra iterations.
claims.evidence_quote: Fixed-depth looping therefore spends additional iterations on many tokens that gain little or even get worse.

claims.claim: TaH2 beats Standard at matched decoding FLOPs on AIME and keeps improving with depth ceiling while Ouro/Huginn plateau.
claims.regime: iso_infer_flop (matched decode FLOPs per response), iso_data
claims.evidence_quote: Existing looped models largely plateau as iteration depth increases, while TaH2's gain over the non-looped baseline grows from +2.8 points at M = 2 to +3.9 points at M = 8 (Figure 1b).

claims.claim: Ouro's exit gate suffers train-inference mismatch because the backbone is trained only at full depth; TaH2 trains on-policy with the decider's own depth decisions.
claims.evidence_quote: Its backbone is trained only at full depth, causing a train–inference mismatch under early exit.

claims.claim: Adaptive depth still costs more than Standard in real serving: 22% more decode FLOPs per token and 30-34% more latency, but better attainable accuracy.
claims.regime: measured wall-clock and FLOPs vs Standard
claims.evidence_quote: Although TaH2 adds 22% decoding FLOPs per token and 30–34% end-to-end latency relative to Standard (Table 2), it still achieves better test-time scaling and higher attainable accuracy

numbers.what: AIME accuracy-compute slope TaH2 vs Standard (points per doubling of decoding FLOPs), 1.7B
numbers.quote: TaH2 improves the accuracy–compute slope by 53% (2.74 vs. 1.79) over the non-looped baseline, exceeding the baseline's peak accuracy by about 3.4 points at matched test-time compute.

numbers.what: slopes of fixed-depth Ouro, adaptive Ouro, Huginn vs Standard
numbers.quote: Fixed-depth Ouro, adaptive Ouro and Huginn yield slopes of 2.12, 2.27 and 2.26 accuracy points per compute doubling, versus 1.79 for Standard

numbers.what: fraction of tokens barely changed / worse after extra iterations (Ouro iter1->2, Huginn iter1->3)
numbers.quote: For Ouro and Huginn, respectively, 52.3% and 33.5% of tokens change by at most 10−3 , while 21.7% and 15.9% become worse by more than this threshold.

numbers.what: AIME peak at 32K: Standard saturates vs TaH2 at same compute
numbers.quote: Standard saturates at 12.0% with 191.7 TFLOPs per response, whereas TaH2 reaches 15.4% at the same compute, 3.4 points higher.

numbers.what: 10-benchmark average gain of TaH2 over Standard vs depth ceiling
numbers.quote: Across the ten benchmarks (Table 1), TaH2's average gain over Standard grows from +2.9 points at M = 2 to +4.8 at M = 8, whereas Huginn and Ouro stay close to Standard

numbers.what: runtime overhead of TaH2 vs Standard
numbers.quote: Although TaH2 adds 22% decoding FLOPs per token and 30–34% end-to-end latency relative to Standard (Table 2)

numbers.what: test-time ceiling outside training ceiling (M=8 checkpoint)
numbers.value: ceiling 4: -2.7 to -3.1 points; ceiling 12: unchanged accuracy, +20-27% mean depth
numbers.quote: Lowering the ceiling to 4 reduces accuracy by 2.7–3.1 points across AIME24–26. Raising it to 12 leaves accuracy essentially unchanged while increasing mean depth by 20–27%.

numbers.what: gains at larger scales
numbers.quote: TaH2 outperforms Standard on every benchmark at both sizes, raising average accuracy by 3.2 points at 4B and 2.4 points at 8B.

numbers.what: ablation: uniform decider loss weights
numbers.quote: Weighting all decisions uniformly instead of by gain magnitude causes the largest drop, 3.6 points, and lowers accuracy on all three benchmarks.

numbers.what: post-training tokens at 1.7B
numbers.quote: We train for three epochs with a 16,384-token context, totalling 3.4B training tokens.

numbers.what: Ouro-style exit-gate collapse in post-training (reason Stage I is simplified)
numbers.value: every token exits after the first iteration
numbers.quote: To avoid gate collapse in post-training, where every token exits after the first iteration, we simplify Stage I

limitations: More training FLOPs than standard SFT (lookahead iterations); studied only under SFT, not RL or on-policy distillation; adaptive model still costs more FLOPs and latency per token than the non-looped baseline.
survey_notes: Key evidence that a learned per-token halting decider is not free: even at its best TaH2 costs 1.22x decode FLOPs and 1.30-1.34x latency vs non-looped (Table 2), and Ouro-style exit gates trained on a frozen full-depth backbone fail to beat Standard at matched compute (post-training regime only; contrasts with Ouro's pretraining claims). Reports Ouro-style gate collapse in post-training (every token exits after iteration 1) and fixes Ouro Stage I by removing the gate. Supervised-label alternative to ACT/PonderNet penalties and to MoR capacity routers; ablation shows TaH-style mismatch labels and sampled (stochastic) training decisions are worse than gain labels and deterministic on-policy decisions. Inference ceiling above the trained M gives no gains (no depth extrapolation), consistent with train-test depth mismatch limits. Ouro and Huginn here are re-implementations post-trained from Qwen3, not the public checkpoints, so comparisons are matched.

title: CHASE: Cache-Hole-Adapted Skip Exit for Looped State-Space Language Models
relevance_reason: Looped Mamba / hybrid LMs pretrained from scratch with Ouro-style token-level exit gate; identifies and fixes the state-skip (cache-hole) mismatch so exits yield real savings.
one_sentence: Loops Mamba-2 and hybrid blocks; under iso-parameter they help, under iso-FLOP deeper non-looped wins perplexity; Ouro's exit gate saves nothing unless trained on skipped-state (cache-hole) passes, which CHASE does, halving executed loops.
key_contributions: Iso-parameter and iso-FLOP (equal effective depth) study of Looped Mamba-2, Looped LLaMA2 and hybrids on Mano, p-hop and 100B-token pretraining.
Identifies cache-hole mismatch: Ouro-style gate trained on dense trajectories breaks when exited tokens are actually skipped in a recurrent-state backbone (perplexity explodes).
CHASE continued training on cache-hole-consistent forward passes with sampled exit thresholds; measures real prefill speedups and the ragged-halting gap between average exit depth and wall-clock.

setup.model_sizes: 140M and 370M (limited to models up to 370M parameters)
setup.train_tokens_or_data: Nemotron-ClimbMix; 100B tokens (Table 3), 150B tokens + 5.2B Stage-1 gate + CHASE + 1.2B Stage-2 gate (Table 4)
setup.loops_train: R = 4 recurrent steps for exit-gated models; N x R grids (4x6, 6x4, 12x2 vs 24x1) for iso-FLOP study
setup.loops_test: threshold q controls exits; average executed loops ~2.04-2.76 of 4
setup.baselines: non-looped Mamba-2 / LLaMA2 at same parameters, deeper non-looped at same effective depth, fixed-loop models, stock Ouro two-stage gate
setup.benchmarks: Mano, p-hop induction, validation perplexity, seven downstream tasks (including BoolQ)

claims.claim: Under strict iso-FLOP (equal effective depth), deeper non-looped models keep a validation-perplexity advantage, though looped models stay competitive downstream with fewer parameters.
claims.evidence_quote: looped models remain competitive on downstream benchmarks with substantially fewer distinct parameters, although deeper non-looped models retain an advantage in validation perplexity under strict isoFLOPs comparisons.

claims.claim: The stock Ouro gate on Looped Mamba saves no compute (it only relocates readout); actually skipping loops makes perplexity explode, while CHASE stays within +3-4% of full-compute perplexity.
claims.regime: iso_param (same backbone, same Stage-1 and Stage-2 training, differ only in cache-hole adaptation)
claims.evidence_quote: the stock Ouro Stage-2 gate's validation perplexity explodes—by up to +4788% (from 12.2 to nearly 600) and erratically—because a skipped loop leaves the recurrent Mamba state without its update.

claims.claim: Naively truncating a fixed-loop model at inference fails because intermediate recurrent states are miscalibrated with the LM head; adaptive per-token exits beat a shared fixed exit depth at comparable executed loops.
claims.evidence_quote: Naively truncating a fixed-loop model at inference time is therefore not a viable way to save computation, and no single forced depth is optimal for all tasks.

claims.claim: Average exit depth overstates wall-clock speedup (ragged halting); savings appear only when prefill is compute-bound and memory is not reduced.
claims.regime: measured wall-clock prefill throughput, matched thresholds
claims.evidence_quote: The average exit depth therefore overstates the achievable speedup—the ragged-halting effect that motivates the fixed-iteration choice of Deng et al. (2026).

numbers.what: CHASE 140M Mamba-2 downstream avg and executed loops vs full-compute Ouro gate and fixed loop4
numbers.value: 38.82 at 2.15 loops vs 38.86 at 4 loops vs 37.79
numbers.quote: it reaches 38.82 Avg. at only 2.15 executed loops, essentially matching the fullcompute Ouro gate (38.86 Avg. at 4 loops) and exceeding the fixed loop4 baseline (37.79).

numbers.what: CHASE 370M downstream avg at executed loops vs Ouro gate and fixed loop4
numbers.quote: CHASE reaches 38.32 Avg. at 2.04 executed loops, surpassing the full-compute Ouro gate (37.58) and approaching the strongest fixed-depth model (loop4, 38.51) at about half its compute.

numbers.what: wall-clock prefill speedup of CHASE vs full computation
numbers.value: no faster at batch 1; 1.8x at batch 64
numbers.quote: CHASE is no faster than full computation at batch 1, and reaches 1.8× at batch 64, with larger models benefiting more than smaller ones (Section 5.4).

numbers.what: batch-size dependence of speedup
numbers.quote: at batch 1 packing gives no benefit (0.95– 0.97× at 140M) because the prefill is latencybound, whereas at batch 64 CHASE reaches 1.73× (140M) and 1.83× (370M) at q=0.2.

numbers.what: ragged-halting gap: implied vs measured speedup at 370M, q=0.4
numbers.value: 2.76 avg loops implies 1.45x; measured 1.29x at batch 16
numbers.quote: q=0.4 at 370M exits after 2.76 loops on average, implying 1.45×, while the measured value is 1.29× at batch 16—which quantifies the raggedhalting gap.

numbers.what: naive forced two-loop inference downstream avg
numbers.quote: Naively forcing two loops yields only 37.59 and 34.57 Avg. at 140M and 370M, respectively, because intermediate recurrent states are miscalibrated with the language-modeling head.

numbers.what: pretraining tokens for iso-FLOP study
numbers.quote: Models in Table 3 are pretrained for 100B tokens, corresponding to 50,000 iterations, from the Nemotron-ClimbMix dataset

numbers.what: Cache-hole adaptation: fraction of holed positions and sampled exit depth distribution
numbers.value: hp=0.5; exit depth ~ Uniform[1.85, 3.45] over R=4
numbers.quote: we continue training with holed forward passes that hole a fraction hp=0.5 of positions and, for each hole, sample a target exit depth uniformly in [1.85, 3.45] over the R=4 recurrent steps

limitations: Models only up to 370M and 100B-150B tokens; synthetic reasoning tasks; cache-hole adaptation only for pure Looped Mamba (hybrid attention KV holes unhandled, hybrids reported only with full-compute gate); global thresholds q rather than optimized per-token/example allocation; packing saves compute not memory.
survey_notes: Central caution for the loop-count section: an Ouro-style entropy-regularized exit gate trained on dense full-depth trajectories saves zero FLOPs unless the backbone is trained on skipped-state trajectories (train-test mismatch made explicit; for SSMs the mismatch is catastrophic, up to +4788% PPL). Agrees with TaH2 (2609.35748) that Ouro's gate on a full-depth-trained backbone has a train-inference mismatch. Reports measured wall-clock rather than only average loops, and quantifies that average exit depth overstates speedup (1.45x implied vs 1.29x measured); no speedup at batch 1; no memory savings. Iso-FLOP result (deeper non-looped wins perplexity) agrees with Saunshi et al. Earlier arXiv title: 'Looped State-Space Language Models with Adaptive Exit-State Selection' (same DOI). Not a transformer: SSM backbone.

title: Fixed-Point Reasoners: Stable and Adaptive Deep Looped Transformers
relevance_reason: Looped transformer that halts when its hidden state reaches a fixed point (training-free convergence rule) and compares against TRM's learned ACT halting.
one_sentence: FPRM fixes signal propagation in deep looped transformers (pre-norm plus residual scaling, damped iteration) and halts per input when the relative fixed-point residual drops below a tolerance, adapting compute to difficulty better than TRM's ACT head.
key_contributions: Pre-norm looped transformer stabilised with layer-wise and iteration-wise residual scaling; damping factor eta with patience-based decay to suppress oscillation around the fixed point.
Fixed-point residual r_i below tolerance as an end-to-end, module-free halting signal; truncated BPTT with deep supervision, with exponential-decay bound on truncated-gradient error.
Evidence that ACT halting in TRM halts too early or too late and only some seeds learn to adapt, while fixed-point halting scales compute smoothly with difficulty.

setup.model_sizes: 7M parameters (compared with 7M-27M HRM/TRM/URM/Attractor/EqR baselines)
setup.train_tokens_or_data: Sudoku-Extreme (1000 puzzles x1000 augmentation), Maze-Hard (1000), ARC-1/ARC-2, A5/S5 state tracking up to 32 updates
setup.loops_train: loop windows of k iterations (truncated-BPTT length) with deep supervision until the optimizer detects a fixed point
setup.loops_test: until residual < tolerance (0.1) or step size too small, under max budgets (e.g. 320, 4788, 70k effective layers)
setup.baselines: TRM with and without ACT (their runs), TRM+conv, HRM, URM, Attractor Model, EqR (mostly reported numbers)
setup.benchmarks: Sudoku-Extreme, Maze-Hard, ARC-AGI-1, ARC-AGI-2, A5, S5

claims.claim: Convergence of the hidden state to a fixed point can be used directly as the halting signal, needing no learned halting module.
claims.evidence_quote: let the model loop until its hidden state converges to a fixed-point, and use the convergence itself as the halting signal. Unlike ACT, the fixed-point halting mechanism requires no external module

claims.claim: Learned ACT halting in TRM is unreliable: it halts too early or too late, and on S5 only a few seeds learn to adapt.
claims.evidence_quote: In contrast, TRM with its ACT halting mechanism either halts too early, resulting in lower performance, or too late, using excessive compute.

claims.claim: On A5/S5 length generalization at length 128, FPRM keeps high accuracy while scaling compute with length; TRM+conv+ACT drops on A5 and uses more compute on S5.
claims.regime: matched compute budget of 320 effective layers
claims.evidence_quote: On S5 , it reaches 96.2% ± 3.2%, but uses substantially more compute than FPRM; moreover, only a few seeds learn to adapt, while the others exhaust the full compute budget.

title: Per-Token Fixed-Point Convergence in Depth-Recurrent Transformers
relevance_reason: Huginn-style randomized-depth LM; measures per-token fixed-point convergence and compares a training-free KL convergence exit with a learned router on the same frozen backbone.
one_sentence: On a 135M-class randomized-depth recurrent LM, hidden states converge to per-token fixed points at varying depths; a training-free successive-output KL exit reaches uniform depth-8 loss at 4.94 average loops, while a trained linear router saves nothing.
key_contributions: Per-token measurement of recurrence: successive-output KL and state change decay to a fixed point; median token converges by loop 6, ~10% still updating at loop 8; depth ordered by token type.
Post-hoc allocation on a frozen backbone: training-free KL-threshold exit beats an oracle-labeled linear router (same model labels) at matched average depth.
Explicit savings scoping: average depth as FLOP proxy (38%), best-case wall-clock ~1.5x, realized ~0% in the masking harness; saturation at training-mean depth hypothesis.

setup.model_sizes: S0: 12.9M unique non-embedding (31.8M total); S1: 29.0M unique non-embedding (57.3M total), 135M-class compute at mean depth
setup.train_tokens_or_data: S0: 400M tokens TinyStories; S1: 12.9B tokens FineWeb-Edu, single seed
setup.loops_train: per-step r ~ round(LogNormal(log r_bar, 0.5)) clamped to [1, r_max]; S0 r_bar=4, r_max=16; S1 r_bar=8, r_max=32; truncated BPTT k=4/8
setup.loops_test: uniform 1-32; adaptive exit up to r_max
setup.baselines: uniform depth (A0), oracle-labeled linear router (A2), fixed-depth-4 trained control (S0), SmolLM2-135M ceiling reference
setup.benchmarks: validation loss (FineWeb-Edu, TinyStories); no downstream tasks

claims.claim: A training-free per-token convergence exit outperforms a router trained to predict convergence from the same model.
claims.regime: same frozen backbone, matched average depth
claims.evidence_quote: a training-free rule that halts each token once its output stabilizes attains uniform depth-8 quality at 4.94 average loops (a 38 percent reduction in average depth)

claims.claim: The learned linear router needs essentially full depth and gives no saving.
claims.evidence_quote: The trained router A2 needs average depth 7.99 to reach the same quality, yielding no saving, and underperforms A1 across the range.

claims.claim: Randomized-depth training gives depth robustness; a fixed-depth-trained model is sharply peaked at its training depth.
claims.evidence_quote: A model trained at a constant four loops (S0) is sharply peaked at its training depth: loss 1.97 at r = 4 but 6.01 at r = 1 and 2.50 at r = 16.

claims.claim: Useful depth saturates at the training-mean depth (hypothesis from two internal points plus Huginn consistency).
claims.evidence_quote: Across our two scales the pattern is exact: trained at mean 4, saturates at 4; trained at mean 8, saturates at 8.

numbers.what: mean successive-output KL at loops 2, 8, 16
numbers.quote: KL is 3.9×10−1 at loop 2, 5.4×10−4 at loop 8, and 8.5×10−6 at loop 16. The state reaches a fixed point.

numbers.what: fraction of tokens still moving (KL > 1e-3) at loops 7, 8, 16
numbers.quote: At loop 7, 33 percent of tokens are still moving; at loop 8, 10 percent; by loop 16, 0.1 percent.

numbers.what: validation loss vs loops (S1)
numbers.value: 3.80 at r=1 to 3.20 at r=8; flat to 32
numbers.quote: Loss falls monotonically from 3.80 at one loop to 3.20 at eight, then stays flat: r = 8, 16, and 32 are 3.202, 3.203, and 3.203.

numbers.what: convergence exit vs uniform at average depth 3
numbers.quote: At average depth 3 the margin is clear (3.231 against 3.272); at average depths 4 through 7 the two are within 0.002 to 0.003 nats, with A1 never higher.

numbers.what: three-point savings bracket
numbers.quote: The three-point bracket is therefore: 38 percent by average depth, about 1.5 times best-case wall-clock, and about 0 percent realized in our harness.

numbers.what: best-case wall-clock uniform r=8 vs r=5
numbers.quote: A matched-depth wall-clock timing (uniform r = 8 against uniform r = 5, the approximate A1 average) gives a 1.48 to 1.51 times speedup across batch sizes 1 to 8

numbers.what: mean exit depth by token class at S1
numbers.quote: Mean exit depth at S1 orders as space 3.58, numeral 3.81, punctuation 4.16, word 4.25.

numbers.what: training sampling distribution of recursion count
numbers.quote: Per optimization step we sample one recursion count, r ∼ round(LogNormal(log r̄, 0.5)) clamped to [1, rmax ], and apply it to the whole step.

numbers.what: SmolLM2-135M ceiling vs recursive model
numbers.quote: Evaluated under our S1 harness, SmolLM2-135M scores 2.66 nats against the recursive model's 3.20 at r = 8, a gap of 0.54 nats.

limitations: Single 135M-class scale and single seed for S1; no FLOP-matched dense baseline; average depth is only a FLOP proxy, realized throughput ~0% in teacher-forced masking harness; KV cache for per-token exit at decode not stress-tested; no downstream evaluation; quality does not improve beyond training-mean depth.
survey_notes: Direct contradiction with learned routing (MoR 2507.10524, TaH2 2609.35748): on a randomized-depth backbone a zero-parameter KL threshold beats a trained router (7.99 vs 4.94 average loops for depth-8 quality), but the router here is a linear probe trained post hoc on a frozen backbone, not jointly trained; TaH2 by contrast reports that jointly trained deciders win. Savings are explicitly a FLOP proxy; best-case wall-clock 1.48-1.51x, realized 0. Agrees with Huginn (2502.05171) convergence-exit observation and with FPRM (2606.18206) that convergence is a usable halting signal. Supports 'saturation at training-mean depth' (no depth extrapolation gains), consistent with TaH2 ceiling-12 result. Cites 2604.21999 for shallow-halt collapse of jointly trained halting. Weights: the reproducibility statement says the final S1 checkpoint is available at the GitHub URL.

title: Adaptive Depth in Looped Transformers: Diagnosing Learned Halting Gates and Trajectory Readouts
relevance_reason: Diagnostic study of PonderNet/Ouro-style learned halting vs fixed-prior depth supervision plus post-hoc confidence/convergence readouts, on synthetic tasks and public Ouro checkpoints.
one_sentence: Shows learned halting gates entangle exit selection with trajectory formation; fixed-prior per-depth loss weighting plus simple post-hoc confidence readouts match or beat jointly trained linear/MLP gates on MANO and are competitive with Ouro's pretrained ponder gate.
key_contributions: Trajectory-readout decomposition: the exit distribution q(.|x) both weights per-depth losses in training and stops at inference; fixed-prior (uniform or truncated geometric) depth supervision separates the two.

On MANO, fixed-prior trajectories with logit-margin/top-1 readouts reach 95-99% accuracy at 1.4-1.6 average loops while jointly trained gates need more depth or never reach the target; re-fitting gates on frozen gate-trained trajectories does not help.
On public Ouro-1.4B/2.6B, post-hoc readouts are competitive with the pretrained ponder gate (higher accuracy in 5/12 pairs, fewer loops in 7/12); latency measured on MANO and estimated on Ouro.

setup.model_sizes: MANO: 4-layer, 4-head, d=512 looped transformer; Ouro-1.4B and Ouro-2.6B public checkpoints
setup.train_tokens_or_data: MANO modular arithmetic (mod 23, up to 10 operations), 50k-example splits; binary parity length 1-40; Ouro evaluated as released
setup.loops_train: maximum recurrent depth T = 6 (MANO), all depths supervised with fixed prior or learned exit distribution; Ouro up to 4 recurrent steps
setup.loops_test: adaptive exits via thresholds, forced exits at each depth
setup.baselines: fixed-depth readout, learned linear and MLP gates (PonderNet-style with KL to prior, beta sweep), Ouro pretrained ponder gate, post-hoc gates on frozen trajectories (PonderNet-style and Ouro Stage-II marginal-utility objective)
setup.benchmarks: MANO, binary parity, MMLU, ARC-Easy, ARC-Challenge, OpenBookQA, HellaSwag, CommonsenseQA

claims.claim: Fixed-prior depth supervision with simple confidence readouts matches or beats jointly trained learned gates; failure stems from the trajectory induced by joint gate training, not gate expressivity.
claims.regime: same backbone and data, matched average exit depth
claims.scale: Ouro-2.6B (checkpoint evaluation); controlled at small MANO model
claims.evidence_quote: Fitting gates on frozen trajectories localizes the failure: it appears to stem mainly from the trajectory induced by joint gate training rather than from limited gate expressivity.

claims.claim: Learned gates require more average depth than fixed-prior readouts to reach target accuracy on MANO.
claims.evidence_quote: Across three seeds, the geometric fixed-prior trajectory paired with logit margin achieves a favorable frontier, requiring only 1.4–1.6 average loops to reach 95% − −99% accuracy. Learned gates consistently require greater depth

claims.claim: On Ouro checkpoints, post-hoc readouts are highly competitive with the pretrained ponder gate, which is not uniformly Pareto-optimal.
claims.regime: same public checkpoint, matched average loops
claims.evidence_quote: In five of the twelve model–benchmark pairs, the selected post-hoc readout achieves higher held-out accuracy than the gate, though several of these differences are small and reported on single runs.

claims.claim: Large KL-to-prior regularisation collapses the learned gate onto a near-fixed-depth operating point.
claims.evidence_quote: large β pulls the exit distribution toward the prior and collapses the gate onto a near-fixed-depth operating point, visible as the gate curve contracting to a small range of average depths.

numbers.what: MANO latency: fixed-prior geometric model, top-1/margin readouts
numbers.quote: top-1 confidence and logit margin maintain 100.0% accuracy while reducing average depth from 6.0 to 1.26 loops, giving 1.36× and 1.29× speedups; predictive KL preserves near-perfect accuracy at 1.11×.

numbers.what: MANO learned gate
numbers.quote: The learned gate reduces average depth from 6.0 to 1.59 loops (1.24×) but operates at lower accuracy (around 75%), so here the fixed-prior trajectory with simple confidence readouts gives a more favorable accuracy–latency tradeoff.

numbers.what: Ouro pretrained gate estimated latency speedups
numbers.quote: The pretrained gate consistently reduces estimated latency, with speedups ranging from 1.24× on CommonsenseQA to 1.58× on ARC-Easy.

numbers.what: Ouro post-hoc vs gate across 12 model-benchmark pairs
numbers.value: fewer loops in 7, better both in 3
numbers.quote: In seven pairs, it uses fewer average recurrent loops, and in three pairs, it improves both accuracy and compute.

numbers.what: MANO geometric prior frontier
numbers.quote: The geometric prior λ = 0.3 yields a favorable frontier, with confidence readouts reaching 99% accuracy at roughly 1.5 average loops.

limitations: Controlled training only on small synthetic tasks (MANO, parity); Ouro checkpoints cannot be retrained so only readouts vary; several Ouro differences are small and single-run; Ouro latency is estimated; average exit depth is the main compute metric.
survey_notes: Key 'learned gate vs training-free readout' evidence: agrees with 2607.14427 (convergence exit beats trained router) and FPRM 2606.18206, but adds the mechanism: joint gate training damages the trajectory (learned-gate MANO model tops out ~76% final-loop accuracy vs 100% fixed prior). Contrasts with TaH2 2609.35748 which argues jointly trained, on-policy gain-labeled deciders beat Ouro's gate; TaH2's decider uses supervised labels, not a PonderNet-style weighting, so both can hold. Also notes PonderNet-style post-hoc gate beats Ouro Stage-II marginal-utility objective, which exits later. Ouro savings are estimated latency at batch-level per example, Ouro checkpoints are used as released (no retraining). Sequence-level (MANO answer) and token-level (Ouro) exits. Authors explicitly do not claim this is evidence against learned halting in principle.

title: Universal Transformers Need Memory: Depth-State Trade-offs in Adaptive Recursive Reasoning
relevance_reason: Single-block Universal Transformer with per-token ACT on Sudoku-Extreme; documents an ACT router initialization trap (shallow-halt collapse) and ponder-penalty warmup savings.
one_sentence: A 3.2M single-block UT with ACT and learned memory tokens on Sudoku-Extreme: memory tokens are necessary, standard ACT halting-bias initialization traps most runs in shallow halting, deep-start bias -3 fixes it, and lambda warmup cuts ponder steps 34%.
key_contributions: Router initialization trap: zero bias and Graves' positive bias both settle into a shallow-halt equilibrium; >70% of runs fail; deep-start bias -3 resolves it; ablation with RMSNorm shows it is inherent to ACT initialization.
Ponder penalty applied directly collapses halting even with deep start; lambda warmup keeps accuracy with 34% fewer ponder steps; ACT has far lower seed variance than fixed depth.
Depth-state substitution: more memory tokens lower mean halt depth at fixed accuracy; inference beyond trained depth (2x) improves exact match.

setup.train_tokens_or_data: Sudoku-Extreme
setup.loops_train: up to K = 18 ACT steps per token
setup.loops_test: ACT halting; extended inference up to 64 steps

setup.benchmarks: Sudoku-Extreme exact match

claims.claim: Applying the ponder penalty directly collapses halting even with deep start; warmup of lambda recovers 34% compute at matched accuracy.
claims.evidence_quote: Direct application of the ponder penalty collapses halting even with deep start. Lambda warmup resolves this: the model establishes deep processing during the warmup phase, then the penalty compresses computation to halt ≈ 11.

claims.claim: ACT gives an order of magnitude lower seed variance than fixed-depth processing at similar mean accuracy.
claims.evidence_quote: ACT provides more consistent results than fixed-depth processing (56.9±0.7% vs 53.4±9.3%), and lambda warmup achieves matching accuracy (57.0±1.1%) using 34% fewer ponder steps

claims.claim: Running a lambda-warmup ACT model beyond trained depth improves accuracy, with a sweet spot around 2x training depth and graceful degradation after.
claims.evidence_quote: Running the lambda-warmup model for 36 steps (2× training depth) yields 66% EM, up from 52% at step 17—a 14pp gain from inference-time compute alone, with no retraining.

numbers.what: fraction of runs failing under standard ACT init
numbers.quote: In our setting, >70% of runs fail to escape. We propose deep-start initialization (bias = −3, p ≈ 0.05), which inverts the assumption and resolves the issue.

numbers.what: runs escaping the trap with bias=0
numbers.quote: Bold = escaped the trap (>20% EM). 4 of 13 completed runs succeed; seed 123 never escapes.

numbers.what: lambda without warmup (collapse) vs with warmup: EM and mean halt
numbers.value: 3.8% EM at halt 3.7 (no warmup); 57.0% at 11.4 (warmup) vs 56.9% at 16.4-18.0 (lambda=0)

numbers.quote: the halt-vsT curve is monotonically decreasing (11.60 → 11.50 → 10.29 → 8.25 for T ∈ {8, 16, 32, 64}) at near-constant accuracy on the plateau

numbers.what: small-dataset generalization vs TRM
numbers.quote: the single-block UT memorizes but does not generalize (6–8% vs TRM's 87.4%) on the 1K-example protocol

limitations: Single task (Sudoku-Extreme); single-block UT only; 3.2M model, no parameter-matched comparison to TRM (7M); fails to generalize in the 1K-example protocol; savings counted in ponder steps, no FLOP or wall-clock measurement.
survey_notes: Primary evidence for 'collapse to shallow depth' failure mode of jointly trained ACT halting: initialization traps (>70% runs fail) and direct ponder penalty collapse (halt 3.7, 3.8% EM). Cited by 2607.14427 as [5] with a different author ('Csordás et al.') and title ('...in recurrent language models'): the actual paper is by Grigory Sapunov and is about Sudoku-Extreme, not language models; flag citation error. Savings reported only as mean ponder steps (-34%), no FLOPs or wall-clock. Unlike TaH2 and 2607.14427 (no gains beyond trained depth), this ACT model gains +14pp at 2x training depth via step-embedding wraparound, a train-test depth extrapolation counterexample at toy scale. ACT is per-token (81 cells plus memory tokens).

title: AdaPonderLM: Gated Pondering Language Models with Token-Wise Adaptive Depth
relevance_reason: Whole-stack recurrent (PonderLM-style) LM pretrained with learned token-wise halting gates.
one_sentence: Adds iteration-specific sigmoid halting gates with a monotonic mask, a bottom-K ponder penalty and KV reuse for halted tokens to PonderLM; cuts inference FLOPs from 4x to 3.7-3.8x of the backbone at roughly matched perplexity.
key_contributions: Self-supervised token-wise halting learned during pretraining via per-iteration MLP gates, threshold tau=1e-4, persistent monotonic mask, and a bottom-K gate penalty with warmup.
KV reuse for halted tokens so train and test computation match and Flash-Attention compatible pruning is possible.
Iso-FLOP comparison showing learned per-token policy beats uniform and geometric fixed pruning distributions.

claims.evidence_quote: AdaPonderLM reduces inference compute at about 10% while maintaining comparable language modeling perplexity and competitive downstream accuracy

title: LoopFormer: Elastic-Depth Looped Transformers for Latent Reasoning via Shortcut Modulation
relevance_reason: Looped decoder LM trained for budget-conditioned (elastic) loop counts via time/step-size conditioning and shortcut consistency.
one_sentence: Conditions each loop on normalized time and step size (adaLN-style) and trains with a sampled shorter trajectory plus stop-gradient consistency to the full trajectory, giving one ~1B-config looped LM usable at any user-chosen loop budget.
key_contributions: Shortcut-modulated looped Transformer conditioned on (t, delta t) so coarse trajectories approximate the full L-step route.
Training objective L_L + 0.1 L_S + 0.1 L_cons with shortcut length S ~ U{1..L-1} and a random step schedule; elastic inference without retraining.
Representation diagnostics (curvature, anisotropy, entropy, CKA) showing early-exit looped baselines stagnate across loops while LoopFormer keeps evolving; schedule choice at fixed budget matters.

setup.train_tokens_or_data: 25B tokens of deduplicated Pile
setup.loops_train: full L plus one sampled shortcut length S ~ Uniform{1,...,L-1} per batch
setup.loops_test: any budget M <= L (e.g. 2, 4, 8 loops for 3x8)
setup.baselines: non-looped Base (24x1, 12x1, 6x1, 3x1), Base-Loop (Saunshi), TMLT, Naive-Loop-EE, Base-Loop-EE-Cons, TMLT-EE
setup.benchmarks: Perplexity on Pile, FineWeb-Edu, OpenWebText; zero-shot COPA, HellaSwag, LAMBADA, OBQA, PIQA, RACE, SciQ, ARC, SIQA, WinoGrande

claims.claim: Looped models trail iso-FLOP non-looped baselines on perplexity; LoopFormer closes much of the gap and beats fixed-depth looped variants.

claims.evidence_quote: looped models trail non-looped baselines on perplexity, reflecting the role of parameters in memorization. However, LoopFormer closes much of this gap, surpassing even fixed-depth looped variants.

claims.claim: Naive early exiting in looped models produces stagnant late-iteration representations (high cross-step CKA, flat curvature/entropy); LoopFormer keeps evolving.
claims.evidence_quote: Early-exit looped baselines show flat trajectories on all three metrics and high CKA, indicating stagnation.

claims.claim: At a fixed loop budget, the choice of step schedule changes results substantially; best schedules take coarse steps early and fine steps late.
claims.evidence_quote: Despite identical compute, performance varies across schedules (spread ∼1.4 perplexity and ∼1.3 accuracy points).

claims.claim: Fixed-loop looped models collapse when evaluated off their training depth, which motivates elastic training.
claims.evidence_quote: Once trained, their representations collapse when evaluated at shorter or longer depths, since those settings are off-distribution Bae et al. (2024); Fan et al. (2024).

builds_on: Saunshi et al. 2025 (Reasoning with latent thoughts)
survey_notes: Canonical budget-conditioned / elastic-depth method. Savings are not measured as adaptive reductions: user picks the budget; FLOPs measured by kL proxy; only training overhead measured in wall-clock. Its 'Naive-Loop-EE' baseline is described as akin to Huginn-style recurrent depth (without sandwich norm or random init state) and is found to stagnate across loops, which is in tension with Huginn's report of continued gains with more test-time recurrence; but the baseline is small-scale (25B tokens) and the authors' reimplementation. Explicitly rejects per-token halting/routing (MoR, UT ACT) in favor of user budgets. Lowest-budget results are worse than both iso-FLOP and iso-param non-looped baselines on perplexity, so 'elastic' does not mean free at small budgets; the paper's claim 'matches vanilla at low budgets' holds for average accuracy (40.36 vs 40.93) not perplexity. Shortcut-length sampling distribution: uniform over {1..L-1}, plus uniform random step schedule. Successor: T-LoopFormer (2609.15160).

title: T-LoopFormer: Token-Level Elastic-Depth Looped Transformers for Latent Reasoning with Dynamic Routing
relevance_reason: LoopFormer extended with a token-choice router assigning per-token loop counts plus a recursion-wise KV cache.
one_sentence: Adds a softmax-over-depths token-choice router (decided once from the token's initial embedding, threshold 0.5) and per-loop KV caches with gather-scatter to LoopFormer; reports average depth 3.69 of 8 loops, lowest decode latency, and lowest training memory.
key_contributions: Token-choice router mapping the initial hidden state to a distribution over depths; cumulative probability > 0.5 keeps a token active, giving nested monotone active sets.
Recursion-wise KV cache (one cache per loop, attention restricted to same-loop entries) and gather-scatter compaction for training and decoding.
Measured TPOT, TTFT and training memory, not only nominal FLOPs.

setup.model_sizes: hidden 2048, 32 heads, 3-layer shared block x 8 loops (3x params) vs 24-layer ~1B non-looped base
setup.train_tokens_or_data: ~25B FineWeb-Edu tokens
setup.loops_train: max L=8 plus a sampled shortcut S ~ U{1..L-1} (LoopFormer objective); router selects per-token depth up to M
setup.loops_test: user max M in {2,4,8}; per-token depth chosen by router (average 3.69 at M=8)
setup.baselines: Base (24x1, 12x1, 6x1), Base-Loop, TMLT, Naive-Loop-EE, Base-Loop-EE-Align, TMLT-EE, LoopFormer (all retrained)
setup.benchmarks: Perplexity FineWeb-Edu and OpenWebText; zero-shot COPA, HS, LAMBADA, OBQA, PIQA, RACE, SciQ, ARC-C, SIQA, ARC-E; TPOT, TTFT, training memory

claims.claim: At the 24x nominal-FLOP budget (3-layer block x 8 loops) T-LoopFormer outperforms the 24-layer non-looped base; at 12x and 6x it underperforms the base but narrows the gap vs other looped models.
claims.regime: iso_data; 'FLOPs' is nominal J x M upper bound, actual per-token loops are fewer (avg 3.69 of 8), so iso_infer_flop is only nominal
claims.evidence_quote: Moreover, at 24× FLOPs, our model outperforms the non-looped base model with 24× parameter.

claims.claim: Token-choice routing plus recursion-wise KV cache yields the lowest per-token decoding latency, below both the non-looped base and LoopFormer (2.24x faster than LoopFormer).
claims.evidence_quote: compared with LoopFormer, our model achieves 2.24× decoding speed faster than LoopFormer, which confirms that the dynamic token-choice routing mechanism and the recursion-wise KV cache are effective in improving inference speed.

claims.claim: Most tokens use at most 4 of 8 loops; depth distribution is long-tailed.
claims.evidence_quote: most tokens require at most 4 loops (average depth is 3.69), and the overall distribution exhibits a long-tail pattern

claims.claim: Depth is fixed from the token's initial hidden state and not recomputed during looping; when the required depth exceeds the max loop limit (low budgets) decoding degrades.
claims.evidence_quote: because the loop count for each token is not recomputed during the looping stage, the token’s understanding of the context may be constrained, leading to degraded reasoning performance

numbers.what: TPOT ms/token: Base 24x1, Base-Loop, TMLT, Naive-Loop-EE, Base-Loop-EE-Align, TMLT-EE, LoopFormer, T-LoopFormer
Training memory MB, same model order
Average per-token depth at 8-loop max on FineWeb-Edu validation
numbers.quote: most tokens require at most 4 loops (average depth is 3.69), and the overall distribution exhibits a long-tail pattern

numbers.what: Ablation: PPL increase without router / without recursion-wise KV cache
numbers.quote: the token-choice router contributes more to generating correct tokens (without router, PPL increases 2.12, without recursion-wise KV cache, PPL increases 0.58)

numbers.what: Gather-scatter: training memory and inference latency increase without it
numbers.quote: without gather-scatter during training, memory will increase 21.9%, which validates that the gather-scatter mechanism can improve the training efficiency and figure 4b shows that without gather-scatter during inference, the inference latency will increase 26.4%

numbers.what: FLOP accounting convention
numbers.value: FLOPs proportional to J x M, ignoring embeddings
numbers.quote: In terms of FLOPS, 24× denotes the product of the number of model layers J and the user-specified inference depth M , F LOP s ∝ J ⊗ M , ignoring embedding/unembedding costs.

limitations: Router conditions only on the initial hidden state (token embedding plus position), and per-token depth is not recomputed during looping; tokens needing more loops than the max degrade, so the model underperforms the non-looped base at 12x and 6x. Small scale (~25B tokens, single architecture). FLOP labels are nominal upper bounds.
survey_notes: Token-level routing successor of LoopFormer. Router has no compute penalty: it is trained only through the task loss via cumulative-probability gradients and an optional STE (App. C), yet averages 3.69 of 8 loops, so pressure to shorten depth must come from the shortcut-trajectory training. Because h(0) = token embedding + positional embedding, the router is effectively context-free (token identity and position), unlike MoR-style routers that act on intermediate states; contrast with MoR (not cited) and ITT. It is one of few papers reporting wall-clock decode latency (TPOT) and training memory; but the '24x FLOPs' label is an upper bound and the routed model actually spends fewer loop-FLOPs, so the 'beats Base 24x1' claim is not iso-compute in the actual sense. Base 24x1 training memory 634,225 MB vs ~93,442 MB for 3x8 looped models is reported as measured; ratio looks large and should be treated cautiously. Its retrained LoopFormer numbers (FWE PPL 21.96) differ from LoopFormer's own report (22.87) since data differ (FineWeb-Edu vs Pile).

title: RecurTrace: Adaptive Latent Reasoning with Loop-Time Memory
relevance_reason: Retrofits a middle-block loop into frozen Qwen3 with loop-time memory attention and an oracle-distilled sequence-level halting head; head-to-head vs ACT, PonderNet, CALM, LoopUS, TaH.
one_sentence: Loops layers 12-14 (or 15-17) of frozen Qwen3 0.6B-8B with Loop Memory Attention over the last three loop states, trains with log-normal-Poisson random depth, and halts per sequence via a head distilled from a loss-improvement oracle; beats fixed depth and ACT/PonderNet/CALM on MathQA.
key_contributions: Loop Memory Attention: each looped layer attends over its own states from up to W=3 earlier loops along loop time, with ALiBi-style loop-distance bias.
Oracle-distilled halting: a pooled-state head trained with BCE against 'a deeper loop lowers loss by delta', no compute penalty or confidence proxy; two-loop floor.
Controlled comparison of halting rules on one backbone: ACT and PonderNet collapse to one loop, CALM overspends, LoopUS-Conf and TaH-Mismatch fall in between.

setup.model_sizes: Qwen3 0.6B, 1.7B, 4B, 8B (frozen base, at most ~2.2% added params)
setup.train_tokens_or_data: about 1.15M direct-answer examples (synthetic, math, multi-hop QA, logic)
setup.loops_train: random depth from clamped log-normal Poisson (mean four, log-space sd 0.5), clamp 8; realized mean ~3.9
setup.loops_test: adaptive with floor Tmin=2 (main) or 1 (per-task), budget Tmax; fixed-depth sweeps 1-16
setup.baselines: same-budget fully fine-tuned no-loop baseline; fixed depths; ACT; PonderNet; CALM top-prob and margin; LoopUS-Conf; TaH-Mismatch; matched-size non-looped adapter; plain looping (ETD)
setup.benchmarks: MathQA (controlled study), GSM8K, MATH, AQUA-RAT, ARC-Challenge, HotpotQA, 14 train-covered tasks, 8 classic benchmarks (ARC, HellaSwag, MMLU, ...), synthetic pointer chasing / symbolic state / arithmetic

claims.claim: Oracle-distilled sequence-level halting reaches 56.9% on MathQA at ~2.0 mean loops, beating the best fixed depth (T=2, 54.7%) by 2.2 points at matched compute and all adaptive baselines.
claims.regime: iso_infer_flop (matched mean loops) on the same looped backbone
claims.evidence_quote: RecurTrace achieves 56.9% accuracy with an average of 2.0 loops, exceeding the best fixed loop depth by 2.2 points at matched compute.

claims.claim: Penalty/prior-based halting (ACT expected-depth penalty, PonderNet geometric prior) attached post hoc to a frozen backbone collapses to one loop for all tested regularization strengths; CALM confidence exit overspends loops.
claims.evidence_quote: Sweeping each baseline’s regularization strength over {0.001, 0.01, 0.1} leaves all six settings at a mean depth of 1.0, showing that the collapse is not tied to one hyperparameter choice

claims.claim: The two-loop floor, not the head, prevents collapse; nearly all items stop at the floor and a few deepened items supply the whole gain.
claims.evidence_quote: The two-loop floor is what prevents collapse, raising the one-loop baseline from 1199 to 1313 correct; on top of it, the learned head adds 53 more by deepening mostly items that benefit.

claims.claim: Fixed-depth accuracy is non-monotone (overthinking): peaks at 2 loops and degrades at 8 and 16, so no fixed budget fits all inputs.
claims.evidence_quote: On MathQA, a 1.7B looped model peaks at two loops with 54.7% accuracy, stays near 53.6% at the eight-loop training clamp, and falls to 47.5% at sixteen.

claims.claim: Without loop memory, plain looping of a pretrained block raises NLL at 1.7B-8B; memory reverses this.
claims.evidence_quote: At 1.7B, 4B, and 8B, plain looping instead raises NLL by 0.07, 0.05, and 0.06 nats. Memory reverses every one of these regressions and lowers NLL by 0.03, 0.03, and 0.02 nats.

numbers.what: MathQA baselines: ACT/PonderNet loops, CALM accuracy and loops, LoopUS-Conf and TaH-Mismatch
numbers.value: ACT/PonderNet 1 loop; CALM 54.1% at 5.6; LoopUS-Conf 55.3% at 3.2; TaH-Mismatch 55.7% at 2.1
numbers.quote: By comparison, ACT and PonderNet collapse to one loop, and CALM reaches only 54.1% with 5.6 loops, while the stronger LoopUS-Conf and TaH-Mismatch baselines reach 55.3% at 3.2 loops and 55.7% at 2.1 loops.

numbers.what: Correctness-oracle ceiling and gap closed
numbers.quote: A correctness oracle that assigns each item the depth at which its greedy answer is correct reaches 61.0%.

numbers.what: Wall-clock runtime vs unlooped baseline by depth (teacher-forced)
numbers.quote: Under our measured teacher-forced setup, runtime is about 1.1× the unlooped baseline at two loops, 1.3× at four loops, and 1.7× at eight loops.

numbers.what: Decode latency at mean depth 2.04
numbers.quote: Under our measured decoding setup, latency at the mean operating depth of 2.04 loops is about 1.1× the unlooped baseline.

numbers.what: Per-task adaptive halting: mean loop reduction vs fixed T=8 while matching best fixed depth
numbers.quote: Adaptive matches or beats Best while cutting mean loops by 65–87%.

numbers.what: Accuracy gain over same-budget fine-tuned baseline by scale (two-loop, no halting)
numbers.quote: Generation accuracy over the combined train-covered and classic suites (22 tasks) improves at all four scales, by 0.6, 1.2, 2.2, and 3.4 points from 0.6B to 8B

numbers.what: Fraction of items stopping at the floor at main operating point
numbers.quote: the hard-easy gap is still positive at +0.06 loops even though 97.3% of items stop at the floor.

numbers.what: Training depth distribution
numbers.quote: The realized distribution has a mean depth near 3.9, and about a fifth of passes run six or more loops

limitations: Halting is sequence-level (one depth per example, decided once from the prompt and reused for every generated token); memory reads only same-position states from a three-loop window; only frozen Qwen3 with direct-answer targets, long-form generation untested; latent looping vs CoT complementary. Main MathQA operating point keeps 97.3% of items at the two-loop floor, so most of the 'adaptive' behavior is the floor.
survey_notes: Strongest controlled head-to-head of halting rules on a single looped backbone. Key contradiction: ACT/PonderNet collapse to one loop here, whereas AdaPonderLM (2603.01914) and PonderNet-style works report working end-to-end halting; the authors themselves scope this as a property of post-hoc penalty-based halting on a frozen backbone, not end-to-end training. Also shows the opposite failure (CALM confidence exit overspends to 5.6 loops; LoopUS confidence 3.2 loops). Overthinking is explicit: fixed-depth accuracy falls from 54.7% (2 loops) to 47.5% (16). Randomized depth training uses Huginn's log-normal Poisson. Reports measured wall-clock (runtime/latency ratios), not just loop counts. Plain looping of a pretrained block (= ETD) hurts NLL at >=1.7B, which contradicts a simple 'more loops help' story and suggests retrofitted loops need state/memory. Halting is per sequence, unlike MoR/TaH token-level policies; TaH-Mismatch is a reimplementation as a baseline.

title: Understanding Dynamic Compute Allocation in Recurrent Transformers
relevance_reason: Controlled study of token-level adaptive recurrence (early depth allocation vs online halting) in a prelude-recurrent-coda Transformer.
one_sentence: Builds ANIRA, a prelude/recurrent/coda model with either an early per-token depth decider (ANIRA-E) or online per-step halting (ANIRA-O), trained with CE plus KL to an exponential depth prior, and tests on difficulty-controlled tasks whether allocated depth tracks complexity.
key_contributions: Complexity-controlled evaluation protocol (MANO, BREVO, CLRS-Text, PCFG LANO) where token-level difficulty is parameterized.

Unified recurrent framework isolating decision timing: early allocation (Gumbel-softmax over depths from prelude state) vs online halting (PonderNet-style conditional exit probabilities, inverse-CDF sampling), same regularizer.

Findings: allocation tracks complexity without supervision, but does not yield extrapolation; early decisions use structural cues, online halting tracks algorithmic state; training has a learn-then-reduce-compute two-phase dynamic.

setup.model_sizes: about 5.1M and 13.7M parameters (synthetic); depth-recurrent Llama (McLeish et al.) with 8 recurrent layers for GSM-Symbolic finetune
setup.train_tokens_or_data: synthetic task instances; about 5B tokens Nemotron-CC-Math-v1-4plus for the natural-language finetune
setup.loops_train: unrolled to max D (6, or 14 for MANO) with per-token sampled exit depth via passthrough
setup.loops_test: deterministic exit (modal depth for E, median/CDF>=0.5 for O)
setup.baselines: fixed-depth D=8 recurrent Llama baseline (GSM-Symbolic); ANIRA-E vs ANIRA-O
setup.benchmarks: MANO, BREVO, CLRS-Text (23 tasks), LANO PCFG, GSM-Symbolic Main/P1/P2

claims.claim: Complexity-aligned compute allocation emerges without difficulty supervision, but does not give algorithmic generalization: accuracy drops sharply at unseen input sizes despite extra compute.
claims.evidence_quote: compute allocation aligned with task complexity can emerge without explicit difficulty supervision, but such alignment does not imply algorithmic generalization: models fail to extrapolate to unseen input sizes despite allocating additional computation.

claims.claim: Decision timing matters: early allocation relies on static structural cues (hub out-degree) while online halting tracks algorithmic execution state, and online halting often reaches lower average depth.
claims.evidence_quote: We further find that early compute decisions rely on static structural cues, whereas online halting more closely tracks algorithmic execution state.

claims.claim: Training shows two phases: compute rises to near maximum while learning, then is reduced while preserving accuracy.
claims.evidence_quote: In the learning phase, both variants rapidly increase their compute allocation, often approaching the maximum, suggesting that the model initially relies on near-full recurrent computation to reduce the task loss.

claims.claim: On natural-language math (GSM-Symbolic), neither variant allocates more depth to harder splits; ANIRA-O cuts mean depth from 8 to about 4.1 with a modest accuracy drop.
claims.regime: iso_param, iso_data vs fixed depth-8 baseline (same finetune)
claims.scale: depth-recurrent Llama (McLeish et al.), size not stated in text
claims.evidence_quote: Neither ANIRA variant allocates more depth on the harder splits.

numbers.what: GSM-Symbolic Main/P1/P2: fixed D=8 baseline accuracy, ANIRA-E accuracy, ANIRA-E mean depth
GSM-Symbolic ANIRA-O accuracy and mean depth (Main/P1/P2)
Model sizes
numbers.quote: In total the ANIRA models with hidden size of 512 have about 13.7M parameters and the models with hidden size of 256 have about 5.1M parameters.

numbers.what: Max recurrent iterations
numbers.quote: We set the maximum number of recurrent iterations to D = 6 for all tasks, except MANO where we use D = 14.

numbers.what: Spearman correlation of expected depth with parse-space expansion (ANIRA-E / ANIRA-O)
numbers.quote: Parse-space expansion Parse convergence Addition operations Multiplication operations +0.666 -0.264 +0.618 +0.645 +0.456 -0.111 +0.463 +0.490

numbers.quote: Compared to a non-adaptive model that utilizes the maximum depth D, ANIRA reduces compute and KV cache memory approximately according to the ratio d/D.

limitations: Small synthetic-task models; savings are an analytic mean-depth ratio, not wall-clock; on natural language the allocation is not interpretable and does not track difficulty; adaptivity does not fix extrapolation failure. Deciders use about 8% of total parameters.

artifacts.weights: https://huggingface.co/smcleish/Recurrent-Llama-3.2-train-recurrence-8 (base model used, from McLeish et al.)

survey_notes: Key analysis paper for the 'does learned depth track difficulty' question. Regularizer is KL(q||p) to an exponential prior p(d) proportional to b^-d, which decomposes into negative entropy plus (log b) times expected depth: an entropy-regularized expected-depth penalty (PonderNet-like). Contrasts with RecurTrace (2609.03379), where such penalty/prior halting collapsed to one loop on a frozen backbone; here, trained end-to-end on synthetic tasks, it learns meaningful allocation (no collapse reported). Shows adaptive depth does not imply length generalization, tempering claims that adaptive halting enables extrapolation. On natural language (GSM-Symbolic) depth does not increase with difficulty (P1/P2), echoing the concern that learned routers on NL may encode spurious cues. Early-decision (ANIRA-E, MoR-like router from shallow state) vs online halting distinction maps onto MoR/T-LoopFormer (decide upfront) vs ACT/Ouro (decide per step). Savings only as mean depth ratio d/D.

title: Towards Distributed Neural Architectures
relevance_reason: Router-based architecture where tokens traverse any sequence of modules (including revisiting the same module and identity skips); emergent weight sharing and compute skipping rather than an explicit loop.
one_sentence: Trains models whose per-step routers send each token to any module (transformer/attention/MLP) or an identity module, so depth, skipping and module reuse are learned; language DNA at GPT-2-medium scale roughly matches dense baselines but learned 30% skipping is no better than a 30% shallower dense model.
key_contributions: Distributed architecture: Nm modules, per-step routers (top-1/top-2), up to smax steps, with MoE, MoD, weight sharing and early exit as special cases.
Compute efficiency induced by identity modules plus a DeepSeek-style autograd-free bias update targeting a skip ratio r (no load balancing).
Path analysis: power-law path distributions, emergent specialization, input-dependent module reuse (interpretable in vision, apparently random in language).

setup.model_sizes: language: GPT-2 medium scale (406M top-1, 433M top-2); vision: ViT-Small scale
setup.train_tokens_or_data: about 21B FineWeb-Edu tokens (language); ImageNet (vision)
setup.loops_train: up to smax token-processing steps (hyperparameter); routing per step
setup.loops_test: same routed steps; identity modules give variable compute
setup.baselines: dense GPT-2 (406M), 30% shallower GPT-2; ViT
setup.benchmarks: validation loss, ARC-E, BoolQ, HellaSwag, LAMBADA, PIQA, RACE, Wikitext ppl; ImageNet accuracy

claims.claim: Trained DNAs are competitive with dense baselines in vision and language, and compute efficiency and parameter sharing can be learned from data.
claims.evidence_quote: We empirically show that (i) trained DNAs are competitive with the dense baselines in both domains and (ii) compute efficiency/parameter sharing can be learnt from data.

claims.claim: Module reuse (weight sharing) emerges without explicit incentive; in language it appears random and the authors suggest discouraging it.
claims.evidence_quote: Consequently we conclude that module reuse is most likely random in the language case.

claims.claim: A top-2 DNA trained to skip 30% of tokens has slightly higher validation loss than a 30% shallower dense GPT-2, i.e. learned skipping does not beat a static compute reduction at this scale.
claims.regime: approximately iso_infer_flop (30% less compute) and iso_data
claims.evidence_quote: GPT-2 (30% shallower) top-2 (30% skip) 2.772 2.784

numbers.what: Validation loss: random, GPT-2 406M, top-1 DNA 406M, top-2 DNA 433M
Validation loss: 30% shallower GPT-2 vs top-2 DNA with 30% skip
numbers.quote: GPT-2 (30% shallower) top-2 (30% skip) 2.772 2.784

numbers.what: Language module reuse with and without skip training
numbers.quote: We find that top-2 model reuses about 50% of the modules, while the model trained to skip reuses ≈ 23%.

numbers.what: Training data
numbers.quote: All models were trained on the FineWeb-Edu Lozhkov et al. (2024) 100B-token subset, for approximately 21B tokens in total

limitations: Small scale (authors say models are too small to absorb FineWeb-Edu and make no reasoning claims); no load balancing and no inference-optimized implementation, so no wall-clock savings; savings are fraction of skipped module applications. Routers fixed per step with cap smax.
survey_notes: Adjacent: generalizes token routing over depth to arbitrary module sequences where looping (reuse of the same module) is one emergent option. Useful as a boundary case for the 'token-level routing' policy: learned 30% skip (loss 2.784) is slightly worse than a static 30% shallower dense model (2.772), a data point against learned routing beating static depth reduction at small scale; contrast with MoR (2507.10524) claims. Language module reuse ~50% appears uninformative (uncorrelated across models), suggesting emergent weight sharing in LMs is not semantically driven at this scale. Compute objective is an identity-module bias controller (target skip ratio), not a differentiable ponder cost.

key: t:think at hard selective latent iterations to improve reasoning language models
title: Think-at-Hard: Selective Latent Iterations to Improve Reasoning Language Models
relevance_reason: Earlier title of 2511.08577 (candidates DOI 10.48550/arXiv.2511.08577).
one_sentence: Duplicate entry; see 2511.08577.
survey_notes: Title-only duplicate of 2511.08577; do not count separately.

title: Think-at-Hard: Dynamic Looped Transformers for Improved Reasoning
relevance_reason: Whole-stack looped LLM (fine-tuned from Qwen3) with a learned per-token iteration decider that triggers a second latent iteration only on hard tokens.
one_sentence: TaH identifies latent overthinking (second iterations flip correct tokens), trains a looped Qwen3 with a static oracle depth policy plus an MLP decider that iterates only ~6-7% of tokens, beating always-iterate and same-data Ouro re-implementations by 3.8-4.4%.
key_contributions: Latent-overthinking analysis and an oracle policy (iterate only if the reference SFT model's first-pass top-1 is wrong) that improves accuracy while skipping 81-88% of iterations.
Duo-causal attention across positions and shallower depths, depth-specific LoRA for d>1, and a lightweight MLP iteration decider.
Two-stage training: backbone SFT under a fixed oracle depth policy, then decider imitation with frozen backbone; on-policy oracles collapse.

setup.model_sizes: Qwen3-Base 0.6B, 1.7B, 4B (one layer pruned to match parameters; TaH+ adds <3% params)
setup.train_tokens_or_data: Open-R1 balanced mixture, 100K samples, SFT 5 epochs
setup.loops_train: Dmax = 2 (main); depth chosen by oracle policy
setup.loops_test: Dmax = 2; decider continuation threshold 0.9 (~6-7% tokens iterate twice)
setup.baselines: Standard Qwen3 SFT, AlwaysThink (always 2 iterations), SoftThink, Ouro architecture re-implemented and fine-tuned on same data
setup.benchmarks: nine benchmarks across math, QA and coding (e.g. GSM8K, MATH500, AMC23, AIME25, OlympiadBench, MMLU)

claims.claim: Latent overthinking: in looped models a second iteration fixes some tokens but flips others from correct to wrong, so uniform extra iterations are wasteful or harmful.
claims.evidence_quote: As shown in Figure 8, while the second iteration corrects 8.7% of predictions, it also flips 2.1% of correct ones into errors.

claims.claim: With identical parameter counts and data, TaH beats always-iterate baselines by 3.8-4.4% while skipping iterations on 93% of tokens, and beats single-iteration Qwen3 SFT by 3.0-3.8%.
claims.regime: iso_param, iso_data (Ouro and AlwaysThink re-trained from same Qwen3 backbone on same data)
claims.evidence_quote: With identical parameter counts, TaH outperforms always-iterate baselines by 3.8-4.4% while skipping iterations on 93% of tokens, and exceeds single-iteration Qwen3 baselines by 3.0-3.8%.

claims.claim: Average depth 1.07 iterations per token gives FLOPs and memory access within 4-5% of the standard model (a FLOP/memory proxy), but measured batch-1 decode latency is still higher than Standard (301.4 s vs 210.6 s), though 2.48x faster than AlwaysThink.
claims.regime: unclear (efficiency at batch size 1 on one A800)
claims.evidence_quote: TaH iterates twice on only 6% of tokens on AIME25, with 1.48× lower memory overhead and 2.48× faster decoding than AlwaysThink, while achieving higher accuracy.

claims.claim: Using an on-policy (dynamically recomputed) oracle during backbone training causes training collapse; a static oracle from a separate SFT model is required to break the policy/backbone circular dependency.
claims.evidence_quote: The dynamic approach recalculates the oracle using the evolving backbone in Equation 5, facing the same coupling challenge and causing training collapse.

numbers.quote: Table 1 shows that the oracle policy improves downstream performance by 2.0-7.3%.

numbers.what: Oracle skips iterations on fraction of tokens; NTP gain
numbers.quote: Surprisingly, the oracle policy, which skips iterations on 81-88% of tokens, further improves accuracy by 2.1%.

numbers.what: Average iteration depth and overhead vs Standard
numbers.quote: On average, TaH performs 1.07 iterations per token. It significantly undercuts the 2.08-2.18× FLOPs and memory access of AlwaysThink, matching the overhead of Standard with only 4-5% additional overhead.

numbers.what: Table 3 (AIME25, 1.7B, A800, batch 1): avg depth / memory GB / latency s / throughput tok/s for Standard, TaH, AlwaysThink
Continuation threshold and fraction of tokens iterated
