numbers.what: Decider imitation accuracy of oracle decisions
numbers.quote: It reaches about 83% accuracy at predicting the oracle’s iteration decisions, as shown in Figure 5.

numbers.what: TaH+ gains (with <3% extra params) over Standard
numbers.quote: TaH+, which adds less than 3% additional parameters, further pushes these gains to 5.3% and 6.2%.

limitations: SFT-only on 100K public samples; main results Dmax=2; decider imitates a heuristic oracle (top-1 mismatch of a reference SFT model) rather than optimizing compute-accuracy; Ouro baseline is a re-implementation fine-tuned on Open-R1, not the released model; measured latency remains above the non-looped model.
venue: Proceedings of the 43 rd International Conference on Machine Learning, Seoul, South Korea. PMLR 306, 2026.
survey_notes: Key paper for overthinking as a failure mode of fixed depth: depth 2 can flip correct tokens, so selective depth improves accuracy, not just cost. Policy training signal is supervised imitation of a hand-defined oracle (first-pass top-1 mismatch of a separate SFT model), not ACT/PonderNet or RL; the authors list RL for the compute-accuracy trade-off as future work. Savings caveat: average depth 1.07 and FLOPs within 4-5% of Standard, yet measured batch-1 latency is 301.4 s vs 210.6 s for Standard (Table 3), so the FLOP proxy overstates wall-clock parity; the speedup claim (2.48x) is only vs AlwaysThink. Ouro comparison is iso-param iso-data (re-implemented, same backbone and data), not the public Ouro checkpoint. Agrees with MoR (2507.10524) that most tokens need minimal depth; differs in that TaH's decider is threshold-adjustable at inference (Fig. 6 robustness), whereas MoR's expert-choice capacity is fixed after training.

title: Accelerating Large Language Model Inference via Early-Exiting Algorithms
relevance_reason: PhD dissertation collecting FREE (early exit), Relaxed Recursive Transformers with early-exit and depth-wise batching, and Mixture-of-Recursions.
one_sentence: Dissertation arguing that per-token early exit creates batching/KV bottlenecks, and that parameter sharing (Recursive Transformers with continuous depth-wise batching) and pretrained recursion routers (MoR) resolve them; RRT exit speedups are simulated from oracle exits.
key_contributions: FREE: shallow-deep early exit with synchronized parallel decoding and Beta-mixture adaptive confidence threshold (non-looped).

Relaxed Recursive Transformers: looped uptraining from dense checkpoints, early-exit post-training with an aggressive loss coefficient on intermediate loops, and hypothetical throughput with continuous depth-wise batching.
Mixture-of-Recursions (same content as 2507.10524).

setup.model_sizes: Recursive Gemma, TinyLlama, Pythia (~1B non-embedding); MoR 135M-1.7B
setup.train_tokens_or_data: RRT uptraining up to 60B tokens (SlimPajama) plus 15B tokens early-exit post-training; MoR on FineWeb-Edu
setup.loops_train: RRT: looping blocks (e.g. 2 or 3 loops); MoR: Nr 2-4
setup.loops_test: oracle exit per token at earliest loop agreeing with final loop (simulation)
setup.baselines: vanilla Gemma/TinyLlama/Pythia; continuous sequence-wise batching
setup.benchmarks: few-shot LM benchmarks; throughput averaged over SlimPajama, RedPajama, PG19

claims.claim: Per-token early exit can paradoxically reduce throughput in batched inference because of synchronization and missing-KV bottlenecks; parameter sharing mitigates this via continuous depth-wise batching.
claims.evidence_quote: they introduce a fundamental conflict: the per-token dynamism intended to save computation often creates system-level bottlenecks that can paradoxically reduce throughput in batched inference.

claims.claim: Standard weighted CE over intermediate loop outputs overemphasizes intermediate representations; an aggressive (small) coefficient on intermediate losses plus self-distillation from the final loop works best.
claims.evidence_quote: The aggressive coefficient strategy successfully maintained final loop output performance while enhancing intermediate output performance. Moreover, incorporating knowledge distillation from detached final outputs further enhanced intermediate performance.

claims.claim: Throughput gains of recursive models with early exit (up to 2.66x over vanilla) are hypothetical, computed from oracle exits (earliest loop matching the final prediction) and simulation, not from a deployed confidence-based exit.
claims.evidence_quote: As developing practical early-exiting algorithms is beyond the scope of this work, we present hypothetical throughput improvements based on an oracle-exiting approach [191, 9].

numbers.what: Hypothetical generation speedup of recursive models vs vanilla (oracle exit + CDB)
numbers.quote: In particular, Recursive models demonstrate up to 2.66× speedup in generation compared to vanilla counterparts.

numbers.what: Simulated early-exit throughput improvement range
numbers.value: up to 2-3x; nearly 4x vs vanilla Pythia
numbers.quote: From our simulation, Early Exits reveal a substantial throughput improvement of up to 2-3× compared to a vanilla Transformer with the same architecture.

numbers.what: FREE early-exit inference speedup (non-looped)
numbers.quote: Experimental results demonstrated that FREE significantly improves inference speed by up to 2.16× and enhances robustness across various generation tasks

numbers.what: Early-exit post-training budget
numbers.quote: For fair comparison, the full-size models (Gemma and Pythia) were also uptrained with 60 billion tokens and then post-trained with 15 billion tokens.

limitations: RRT throughput is simulated with oracle exits; practical confidence-based exit and KV computation for exited tokens are left open (the author notes this); the MoR chapter duplicates 2507.10524.
survey_notes: Use mainly as the explicit statement of the systems problem behind loop-count policies: token-level exits save FLOPs but break batching and leave missing KV entries; looped models allow continuous depth-wise batching. Important caveat for the survey: the RRT early-exit speedups (2.66x, 2-3x, ~4x vs Pythia) are oracle-exit simulations, not measured with a learned or confidence policy; the 'nearly 4x vs Pythia' comparison is unmatched (different model family). Avoid double counting with 2507.10524 (Chapter 4 is MoR). Training note: multi-exit (deep supervision) losses with standard increasing weights hurt the final loop; small intermediate weights plus self-distillation preserve it.

title: Inner Thinking Transformer: Leveraging Dynamic Depth Scaling to Foster Adaptive Internal Thinking
relevance_reason: Per-layer weight-shared inner iterations with MoD-style token routing that selects which tokens get extra thinking steps; compared to Loop baselines at equal parameters.
one_sentence: ITT replaces every other layer with an iterated layer whose per-step linear router keeps the top-rho tokens for another thinking step, with residual accumulation and step encodings; at 162M-466M it beats iso-param Loop baselines with fewer FLOPs and allows elastic selection ratios at test time.
key_contributions: Adaptive Token Routing: per-step importance score with percentile threshold selects tokens for additional iterations (MoD-inspired), with selected-token reweighting.
Residual Thinking Connection (accumulate step outputs) and Thinking Step Encoding.
Elastic inference: token selection ratios can be changed after training to trade FLOPs for perplexity.

setup.model_sizes: 162M, 230M, 466M (LLaMA2-style)
setup.train_tokens_or_data: RedPajama, 50B tokens
setup.loops_train: thinking step scaling x2, x3, x4 in ITT layers (every other layer); fixed selection ratios (e.g. 70% per step for x4)
setup.loops_test: same steps or adjusted selection ratios / removed steps
setup.baselines: Vanilla LLaMA2; Loop variants (whole-layer recurrence for every token) with equal parameters
setup.benchmarks: 11 tasks: SciQ, PIQA, WinoGrande, ARC-E/C, HellaSwag, LogiQA, BoolQ, LAMBADA, MMLU; eval perplexity

claims.claim: At equal parameters and data, ITT x4 improves average accuracy more than the Loop baseline that iterates all tokens (1.7% vs 0.3% at 162M).
claims.evidence_quote: the 162M ITT ×4 configuration improves the baseline by 1.7% with 4-step deep thinking in 50% of layers, while Loop improves only by 0.3% after 4 iterations.

claims.claim: Token routing cuts compute relative to looping all tokens: ITT costs 84% of Loop's FLOPs at 3 steps and 70% at 4 steps (theoretical FLOPs).
claims.evidence_quote: With 3-step deep thinking, ITT incurs only 84% of Loop’s computational cost, dropping to 70% at 4 steps.

claims.claim: Selection ratios trained at fixed values can be changed at inference: raising them lowers PPL, lowering them to 50% keeps PPL near the training config.
claims.evidence_quote: we can flexibly adjust token selections to enhance performance (e.g., 10.21 PPL in the 70%, 70%, 90% setting, 0.31 PPL lower than the training config), or reduce token selections to lower costs with no performance loss

claims.claim: ITT x4 at 162M reaches 96.5% of a 466M Transformer's performance (larger model, same data).
claims.evidence_quote: ITT ×4 -162M model significantly surpasses the 230M Transformer and even achieves 96.5% performance of 466M Transformer.

numbers.what: Data efficiency vs vanilla Transformer
numbers.quote: ITT achieves higher performance with the same FLOPs and saves 43.2% of the training data budget compared to Transformer.

numbers.what: Avg accuracy improvement of ITT over baseline by scale
numbers.quote: The advantages of ITT become clearer as model scale increases, with improvements of 1.7%, 2.1%, and 1.7% for the 162M, 230M, and 466M models.

numbers.what: FLOPs reduction from routing (ablation)
numbers.quote: it achieves more than 50% FLOPs reduction by focusing computation on 50% most critical tokens in each step.

numbers.what: Training budget
numbers.quote: ITT models are trained for 50000 steps (50B token budget). The learning rates were set at 3e-4 for all parameters.

numbers.what: Loss reduction of ITT x4 vs baseline and Loop at 50B tokens
numbers.quote: Notably, ITT ×4 shows a 0.09 loss reduction compared to baseline and 0.4 to Loop at 50B tokens.

limitations: Fixed routing patterns (selection ratios) during training; models only up to 466M; residual thinking connections add backward-pass memory; FLOPs savings are theoretical, no wall-clock reported.
survey_notes: Per-layer variant of token-level routing that predates MoR (2507.10524). The compute budget is a fixed selection ratio per step (percentile threshold), so as in MoR the router decides which tokens, not how many; unlike MoR's reported score saturation, ITT reports that the ratio can be changed post hoc (elastic) with little PPL change, a direct contrast with MoR Sec. 7.1. Savings are FLOP-proxy only. The 'Loop' baseline loops every token at the same parameter count, so ITT-vs-Loop is iso-param, not iso-FLOP; ITT also uses fewer FLOPs. Venue: candidates record lists an ACL 2025 anthology link; the text itself is a preprint.

title: DND: Boosting Large Language Models with Dynamic Nested Depth
relevance_reason: Post-training retrofit that re-applies the same transformer layer to router-selected tokens (one nested extra pass per layer), i.e. token-routed per-layer recurrence.
one_sentence: DND adds a sigmoid token-choice router after intermediate layers of pretrained dense/MoE LLMs; tokens above an adaptively controlled threshold (target 20%) get a second pass through the same layer, fused with the vanilla output, giving SFT gains with ~6% extra FLOPs.
key_contributions: Token-choice threshold routing (avoids expert-choice leakage) with normalized fusion of nested and vanilla outputs, applied in post-training to Qwen3, Llama3.2, Gemma3 and Qwen3-30B-A3B.
Router controlling losses (score dispersion and distribution preservation) to keep scores discriminative and away from sigmoid saturation.
Threshold control from buffer error between expected and actual selection ratio, synchronized with EMA of top-k scores.

setup.model_sizes: Qwen3-1.7B, Llama3.2-1B, Gemma3-1B, Qwen3-30B-A3B (MoE)
setup.train_tokens_or_data: full-parameter SFT on a large synthetic-augmented dataset from a 1-2M-instance seed set
setup.loops_train: at most one extra nested pass per DND layer for selected tokens (layers Ls..Le); target selection ratio 20%
setup.loops_test: same; threshold-based selection
setup.baselines: the same base models with full SFT on the same data; ITT-style SFT at same compute
setup.benchmarks: 17 benchmarks incl. BBH, GPQA, AIME24, MBPP, HumanEval+, LiveCodeBench v5/v6, BFCL v3, C-Eval

claims.claim: Adding DND during SFT improves dense 1-2B models by 1.88-2.61 points and Qwen3-30B-A3B by 0.87 average over SFT alone, with negligible extra parameters.
claims.regime: iso_data, approx iso_param (+0.03M params); not iso-FLOP (+~6% FLOPs)
claims.evidence_quote: DND boosts the performances of the dense Qwen3-1.7B, Llama3.2-1B, and Gemma3-1B by 1.88%, 2.61%, and 2.50% and the MoE Qwen3-30B-A3B by 0.87%, all with a minimal parameter and computing increase.

claims.claim: Reviewing 20% of tokens costs about 6% extra FLOPs (analytic estimate), and measured batch-1 throughput on H100 is 91.6-93.1% of the vanilla model.
claims.evidence_quote: The measurement results in the table show that, while achieving performance improvements, our model consistently reaches 91.6-93.1% of the speed of the vanilla model under different circumstances.

claims.claim: Sigmoid threshold routers saturate when the target selection ratio is extreme, losing discrimination near the threshold; an explicit distribution-preservation loss is needed.
claims.evidence_quote: This issue is particularly pronounced when the target selection ratio is low (e.g., 20%) or high (e.g., 80%), as the model may push many scores into the sigmoid’s saturation regions.

claims.claim: SFT with ITT-style top-p token selection at the same compute gives smaller gains, attributed to train/inference mismatch and leakage of the selection rule.
claims.regime: approx iso_infer_flop (same computation cost, per authors)
claims.evidence_quote: we found that when the SFT is conducted with ITT (Chen et al., 2025) under the same computation cost, the performance improvement is not as pronounced.

numbers.what: Extra FLOPs from reviewing 20% tokens (Qwen3-30B-A3B)
numbers.quote: In conclusion, the DND strategy with a 20% token recalculation ratio results in a modest total computational overhead of approximately 6.27%.

numbers.what: Extra parameters for Qwen3-30B-A3B+DND
numbers.quote: Crucially, these substantial performance gains are realized with a negligible increase of only 0.03M parameters

numbers.what: Qwen3-30B-A3B gains on specific benchmarks
numbers.quote: The impact of DND is most pronounced in Coding and Agent tasks, yielding notable gains of +2.05 on BFCL v3, +1.42 on LCB-v6, and +1.24 on LCB-v5.

numbers.what: Expected token selection ratio chosen
numbers.quote: ablation experiments on the Qwen1.7B model, ultimately setting the ktarget to 20%.

limitations: Evaluated only in post-training (SFT); pre-training/continual pre-training untested; at most one extra nested pass per layer; FLOP overhead is analytic and throughput only batch-1.
survey_notes: Token-routing retrofit at large scale (30B MoE). Direction of the trade is opposite to MoR: MoR uses routing to spend fewer FLOPs than full-depth; DND spends ~6% MORE FLOPs than the base model for accuracy. Policy training signal is the LM loss plus router-shaping losses and a feedback controller on the threshold to hit a target ratio, so like MoR/ITT the average extra depth is a fixed hyperparameter (20%), not learned. Contradiction note: DND states MoR requires training from scratch on over 200B tokens; MoR's text says its pretraining corpus comprises 220 billion tokens, but its runs use 10B-20B tokens or up to 16.5e18 FLOPs, so DND's characterization conflates corpus size with training budget. DND reports ITT-style top-p routing underperforms in SFT due to train/inference mismatch, while ITT reports elastic ratios work (2502.13842); the settings differ (pretraining vs SFT).

title: Dr.LLM: Dynamic Layer Routing in LLMs
relevance_reason: Non-weight-tied pretrained LLMs with per-layer skip/execute/repeat-once routers; repeat is a one-step per-layer loop, but the model is not a looped architecture.
one_sentence: Dr.LLM trains small per-layer MLP routers on a frozen LLM to skip, execute, or repeat each layer once per input sequence, supervised by offline MCTS-found accuracy-preserving paths; it improves ARC/DART accuracy while using about 5 fewer layers per example.
key_contributions: Sequence-level per-layer skip/execute/repeat policy decided once per input on windowed mean-pooled hidden states (KV-cache compatible).
Offline length-aware MCTS that finds accuracy-preserving or improving layer edits under a budget, distilled into routers with focal loss.
Evaluation on six LLaMA-3.2/Qwen-2.5 3B-8B models with in-domain and out-of-domain transfer and wall-clock timing.

setup.model_sizes: LLaMA-3.2 3B and 8B (Base, Instruct), Qwen-2.5 3B/7B models (six backbones); routers 11M-16.8M params
setup.train_tokens_or_data: 4k MCTS-derived execution paths on ARC and DART
setup.loops_train: each layer applied 0, 1 or 2 times (at most a single repeat per block)
setup.loops_test: same action space, decided once per sequence
setup.baselines: base model full depth; prior routing methods (e.g. FlexiDepth, MindSkip, CoLa)
setup.benchmarks: ARC, DART (in-domain); MMLU, GSM8k, AIME, TruthfulQA, SQuADv2, GPQA, PIQA, AGIEval (out-of-domain)

claims.claim: Supervised routers improve accuracy while reducing executed layers: mean +2.25 points and 5.0 fewer layers per example on ARC and DART across six models.
claims.regime: iso_param (frozen base, router adds 0.14-0.56% params); compute measured as layers executed
claims.evidence_quote: On ARC (logic) and DART (math), accuracy improves in all cases, with mean gains of +2.25 percentage points (%p) and 5.0 fewer layers per example across six models.

claims.claim: Measured end-to-end generation time falls 15.3% for 1,000-token sequences, with router cost under 1% of latency.
claims.evidence_quote: Dr.LLM achieves a 15.3% wall-time reduction (29.21 s vs. 34.49 s baseline), while the router adds only 0.27 s per query (<1% of total latency).

claims.claim: Supervision is extremely imbalanced toward execute; plain cross-entropy collapses to always-execute and weighted CE still collapses on repeat, so focal loss is needed for any repeat decisions.
claims.evidence_quote: Plain cross-entropy minimizes error by predicting the dominant execute class, yielding trivial accuracy on skip/repeat. Weighted CE partly compensates, but still collapses on repeat.

claims.claim: Repeats are rare but concentrated in late layers and harder DART levels; out-of-domain transfer costs only 0.85 points on average.
claims.evidence_quote: Repeats are rare overall (1–3% of labels) but occur consistently across all datasets, with higher frequency in more challenging DART levels

numbers.what: Max accuracy gain and layers saved (abstract)
numbers.quote: On ARC (logic) and DART (math), Dr.LLM improves accuracy by up to +3.4%p while saving 5 layers per example on average.

numbers.what: Router label class frequencies
numbers.quote: across the highly imbalanced actions (skip: 7.6%, repeat: 2.3%), while the actual per-layer accuracy reaches 96.8%.

numbers.what: Supervision label counts
numbers.quote: Router supervision is highly imbalanced: nskip = 4,399, nexecute = 120,956, nrepeat = 1,457.

numbers.what: Router parameter overhead
numbers.quote: number of trainable parameters (11M for 3B models, 0.14% of base weights; 16.8M for 8B models, 0.56%), training is efficient and completes within 4 hours

limitations: Repeat limited to one extra pass per layer; supervision depends on gold-answer MCTS on two training datasets; decisions are per sequence, not per token; base model is not weight-tied/looped.
venue: Published as a conference paper at ICLR 2026
survey_notes: Adjacent: shows that even in a non-looped LLM, a learned policy that repeats a few late layers can raise accuracy, consistent with TaH (2511.08577) finding selective extra depth beats uniform depth. Policy training signal is supervised imitation of search-derived oracle paths (like TaH's oracle imitation), not ACT/RL. Clear instance of the collapse-to-default failure mode: with plain CE the router collapses to always-execute. Savings reported both as layers-per-example (proxy) and measured wall time (15.3%).

title: Investigating Recurrent Transformers with Dynamic Halt
relevance_reason: Universal-Transformer depth recurrence with ACT/PonderNet-style halting; proposes sequence-level (global mean-pooled, transition-aware) halting versus token-level halting.
one_sentence: Compares depth-wise (UT) and chunk-wise (TLB) recurrence on ListOps, logical inference, flip-flop and LRA, and proposes Gated UT with a global mean-pooled, transition-aware halting gate that beats token-level halting near-IID but not out of distribution.
key_contributions: Gated Universal Transformer (GUT): global (sequence-level) halting from mean-pooled states, transition-aware halting input [mean(H_{l-1}); mean(H_l)], and gating so positions are not permanently frozen.
Critique of token-level UT halting: many halting decisions, early-halted positions become read-only, and no compute saving until all positions halt.
Empirical runtime analysis of dynamic halting vs fixed upper-bound depth.

setup.train_tokens_or_data: ListOps (length <= 100), Logical Inference (<= 6 operators), flip-flop language modeling, Long Range Arena
setup.loops_train: upper bound of layers (e.g. 10-40 in runtime analysis), dynamic halting with alpha_thresh = 0.999
setup.loops_test: dynamic halting; OOD splits with longer/more complex inputs
setup.baselines: Transformer (xPos), UT with token-level halting (Tan et al. 2023 variant), TLB, GUTLB, ablations of GUT
setup.benchmarks: ListOps (near-IID, length/argument generalization, LRA split), Logical Inference OOD, flip-flop LM, LRA

claims.claim: Token-level halting in UT gives no compute saving until every position halts, while risking some positions halting too early and freezing their memory.
claims.evidence_quote: the token-level halt can limit the writable memory (each position can also be considered as a memory slot with read-write capacities) by halting certain positions too early but without providing any computational saving in return

claims.claim: Replacing GUT's global halt with token-level halting, or removing gating or transition information, severely harms near-IID ListOps accuracy; none of the variants fixes OOD generalization.
claims.regime: unclear (ablations of the same model; parameters not matched across model families)
claims.evidence_quote: Replacing a global halt with a token-level halt in GUT (GUT−Global Halt), removing the gating (GUT−Gate), or removing the transition dynamics information (GUT−Transition) - all harm the performance severely in the near-IID setting

claims.claim: With dynamic halting, GUT training runtime saturates near 5 minutes per epoch as the layer upper bound grows to 30-40, while fixed upper-bound variants grow proportionally; at low bounds a no-halt model can be faster because halting computation adds per-layer cost.
claims.regime: n/a (wall-clock training runtime, same model with/without halting)
claims.evidence_quote: as the upper bound is increased to 30 or 40, the runtime of GUT starts to saturate around 5 minutes, whereas the runtime of other models keeps increasing proportionally with the increasing upperbound.

claims.claim: The ACT-style late-halting penalty requires difficult tuning; beta was tuned on validation and set to 0.1 (0 for Logical Inference).
claims.evidence_quote: Note the weight given to the objective LACT typically requires diﬃcult tuning.

numbers.what: Halting penalty weight and threshold used
numbers.quote: in [1, 0.1, 0.01, 0.001] and set the value as 0.1. We use the same β in other tasks as well, except in Logical Inference, where we found it better to set β = 0. We set αthresh to 0.999.

numbers.what: Training runtime per epoch on ListOps for GUT No Halt Upperbound at 10/20/30/40 layers
numbers.quote: GUT No Halt Upperbound GUT Upperbound GUT 10 20 30 40 2:27 min 4:40 min 6:52 min 9:04 min 3:10 min

limitations: All models remain poor at length generalization (e.g. 100 to 1000 tokens on ListOps); UT/GUT underperform chunk-wise models on flip-flop; parameters not matched across UT and Transformer baselines (authors note matching would need wider layers or MoE); savings reported only as training runtime, no inference FLOPs.
survey_notes: Granularity matters: argues for sequence-level (global) halting over token-level halting in weight-tied recurrence, because token-level exits do not save compute until all tokens halt (unless kernels skip halted tokens) and permanently freeze states. This is a direct counterpoint to token-routing designs (MoR 2507.10524, TaH 2511.08577) that rely on per-token exits plus KV workarounds; the contexts differ (algorithmic encoders vs autoregressive LMs). Also an early report that the ACT ponder weight needs careful tuning. Wall-clock evidence is training runtime only and shows halting overhead can cancel savings at small upper bounds.

title: Adaptivity and Modularity for Efficient Generalization Over Task Complexity
relevance_reason: Universal Transformer with per-token ACT halting plus hypernetwork-generated layer weights; studies generalization to more computation steps than seen in training.
one_sentence: Introduces C-PVR (recursive pointer value retrieval) to test generalization over number of computation steps; parameter sharing plus per-token ACT (UT) generalizes better than deeper fixed transformers, and Hyper-UT adds hypernetwork modularity, using fewer average layers, including on ImageNet.
key_contributions: C-PVR task: number of hops (sequential steps) varies independently of input length; train on 1-4 hops, test up to 9.
Comparison of fixed-depth, ACT-only, parameter-shared, UT (sharing + ACT), UT+FiLM and Hyper-UT.
Hyper-UT matches ViT on ImageNet1k while using far fewer average layers.

setup.train_tokens_or_data: C-PVR with ~2M training examples (~450k per hop count, sequence length 100); ImageNet1k
setup.loops_train: ACT up to a maximum number of layers (e.g. T32 ACT max 32 layers); training hops 1-4
setup.loops_test: ACT; test hops 1-9
setup.baselines: T12, T32, T64, T32 ACT, UT, T32 PS, UT+FiLM, UPT, ViT, U-ViT
setup.benchmarks: C-PVR variants (plain, modulus, with/without scratchpad); ImageNet1k and ImageNet v2

claims.claim: For generalization to more hops than trained, adding layers to a fixed-depth transformer does not help, parameter sharing in depth helps despite fewer parameters, and ACT without sharing only improves efficiency (fewer layers), not accuracy.
claims.regime: unmatched (models differ in params and depth)
claims.evidence_quote: In this particular setting adding an ACT mechanism without parameter sharing does not impact performance at all but it improves efficiency in terms of number of layers.

claims.claim: UT+FiLM and Hyper-UT allocate average depth more efficiently and more in proportion to example difficulty than plain UT.
claims.evidence_quote: We observe, in Figure 3, that UT+FiLM and Hyper-UT are more fair and efficient in terms of allocating compute compared to the UT model (HyperUT being the most efficient).

claims.claim: On ImageNet1k, Hyper-UT matches ViT accuracy while using over 70% fewer layers on average; the authors note layer count is an imperfect efficiency measure because per-layer FLOPs differ.
claims.regime: unmatched (ViT has different per-layer cost and params)
claims.evidence_quote: Though the sheer number of layers is not an adequate measure of efficiency—given that the flops per layer vary across models—we note that, on average, Hyper-UT requires a lower total compute budget per example.

numbers.what: Average compute savings of Hyper-UT vs ViT on ImageNet (via fewer layers)
numbers.quote: HyperUT’s performance matches that of a ViT model but with considerably reduced computational demands (achieving over 70% average savings by effectively using fewer layers).

numbers.what: C-PVR training data size
numbers.quote: In the train set we have around 450k of each number of hops (∼ 2M training examples) and the size of the test sets are 50K.

limitations: Synthetic C-PVR and ImageNet only; savings measured as average layers (FLOPs per layer differ across models); no wall-clock; model sizes not matched.
survey_notes: Evidence that halting and weight sharing play different roles: ACT on an untied stack only saves layers, while weight tying is what yields depth generalization (deeper layers in an untied adaptive model are undertrained, per the authors). Savings are reported as average layers per example, a proxy the authors themselves caveat. Per-token ACT, sequence-level difficulty (hops). Preprint, Apple.

title: PALBERT: Teaching ALBERT to Ponder
relevance_reason: PonderNet-style learned exit on weight-shared ALBERT (a looped encoder), with a deterministic quantile exit rule replacing sampling.
one_sentence: PALBERT fine-tunes ALBERT (and RoBERTa) with PonderNet's variational exit objective but exits deterministically when the CDF of the learned exit distribution passes q (Q-exit) and feeds [h_i, h_{i-1}] to a 3-layer Lambda MLP; it beats sampled PonderNet and PABEE on GLUE.
key_contributions: Q-exit: deterministic exit once the cumulative exit probability exceeds a threshold q, replacing PonderNet's Bernoulli sampling at inference.
Lambda layer reading the transition [h_i, h_{i-1}] with a 3-layer MLP and its own learning rate.
Analysis of the geometric prior parameter and of the q trade-off between underthinking and overthinking.

setup.model_sizes: ALBERT-Base (12 shared-layer evaluations), RoBERTa
setup.train_tokens_or_data: GLUE fine-tuning
setup.loops_train: up to 12 layer evaluations; PonderNet loss with geometric prior lambda_p = 0.1, beta = 0.5
setup.loops_test: Q-exit with threshold q (best q = 0.5)
setup.baselines: ALBERT, ALBERT (9 layers), ALBERT PABEE, ALBERT PonderNet (sampling and closed-form expectation); RoBERTa counterparts; all re-implemented
setup.benchmarks: GLUE (SST-2, RTE, QNLI, CoLA, MRPC, MNLI, QQP, STS-B)

claims.claim: PonderNet's sampled exit causes high variance in exit index and poor accuracy; even when the prior mode is the last layer, sampling exits from one of the first 10 layers in almost half the cases.
claims.evidence_quote: Even if λ is low enough so that the mode of distribution is the 12-th layer, in almost half of the cases, the sampling criterion forces the model to exit from one of the first 10 layers.

claims.claim: PALBERT has the best macro GLUE score among early-exit methods (above PABEE and sampled PonderNet) and is comparable to full-depth ALBERT, but does not beat plain ALBERT on every task.
claims.evidence_quote: Vanilla ALBERT outperformed PABEE on most tasks and is comparable to PALBERT, while the latter has the highest score averaged across all tasks (see Macro column in Tables 2, 3).

claims.claim: The Q-exit threshold trades underthinking against overthinking: q = 0.5 is best; larger q often forces all 12 layers and lowers accuracy, smaller q speeds up but underthinks.
claims.evidence_quote: We observed that exiting models with q = 0.5 shows the best overall performance for different tasks. Making q greater than 0.5 leads to a reduction in accuracy and can often force models to evaluate all 12 layers of ALBERT-Base.

claims.claim: Results depend strongly on the geometric prior over exit layers, which the authors name as the main limitation; at the best RTE prior the model mostly exits at the last layer.
claims.evidence_quote: dependency on the explicit prior distribution could be seen as the main limitation of the proposed method, since treating the exit layer index as a latent variable justified its prior distribution.

numbers.what: GLUE test macro scores: PABEE / PonderNet / PALBERT (last three values of the interleaved row)
GLUE test row for full ALBERT (last value is macro)
Prior parameters swept
numbers.quote: We followed the experimental setup from the previous sections and trained models with λ ∈ [0.1, 0.15, 0.25, 0.5].

limitations: Strong dependence on the geometric prior; no theoretical justification for q = 0.5; does not beat plain ALBERT on some GLUE tasks; speed reported only as relative speed-up curves vs full 12-layer inference (no absolute FLOPs/latency numbers in text).
venue: 36th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2022).
survey_notes: Earliest clean evidence in our set that the PonderNet exit RULE at inference matters as much as the training objective: sampling the exit index is harmful; a deterministic CDF threshold fixes most of it. Same transition-aware gate input idea ([h_i, h_{i-1}]) as 2402.00976's transition-based halt. Sequence-level exit (classification). Prior sensitivity echoes ponder-cost tuning difficulty reported by 2402.00976. Overthinking is explicitly named (overconfidence in wrong predictions at full depth), consistent with later LM findings (TaH 2511.08577).

key: t:leveraging relaxed equilibrium by lazy transition for sequence modeling
title: Leveraging Relaxed Equilibrium by Lazy Transition for Sequence Modeling
relevance_reason: Per-token modulation of iterative refinement on top of a Universal Transformer, aiming at a relaxed equilibrium (abstract only).
one_sentence: Lazy transition scales how much each token's representation is updated at each UT iteration, so less ambiguous tokens are refined less and the model oscillates around a relaxed equilibrium; reported gains on MT, pre-training, Learning to Execute and LAMBADA.
key_contributions: Lazy transition mechanism that adjusts the significance of iterative refinements per token on a UT.
Equilibrium-inspired per-token unequal processing in depth.
Evaluation on machine translation, pre-training, Learning to Execute, LAMBADA.

setup.baselines: baseline models including UT (per abstract)
setup.benchmarks: machine translation, pre-training, Learning to Execute, LAMBADA

claims.claim: Tokens differ in how much refinement they need, but UT processes all tokens equally in depth; lazy transition makes per-token refinement unequal.
claims.evidence_quote: Our lazy transition is deployed on top of UT to build LT (lazy transformer), where all tokens are processed unequally towards depth.

claims.claim: LT outperforms baselines on machine translation, pre-training, Learning to Execute and LAMBADA (comparison regime not stated in abstract).
claims.evidence_quote: Our experiments show that LT outperforms baseline models on several tasks of machine translation, pre-training, Learning to Execute, and LAMBADA.

survey_notes: Abstract only (no arXiv id, no full text). Candidates record venue field: 'Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics' (DOI 10.18653/v1/2022.acl-long.208). From the abstract it is unclear whether lazy transition saves compute (skipping iterations) or only rescales updates; it may be a soft per-token gating of refinement magnitude rather than a halting policy. Classified as convergence-style (relaxed equilibrium) with that caveat.

key: t:how many layers and why an analysis of the model depth in transformers
title: How Many Layers and Why? An Analysis of the Model Depth in Transformers
relevance_reason: Weight-tied ALBERT variant with per-token adaptive number of layers; analyses which tokens get more iterations (abstract only).
one_sentence: Builds an ALBERT variant that adapts the number of (tied) layers per token and analyzes iteration counts during pre-training, fine-tuning and inference, finding that difficult or task-crucial tokens receive more iterations.
key_contributions: Per-token adaptive depth in weight-tied ALBERT, viewed as iterative refinement.
Token-level analysis of iteration counts across pre-training, fine-tuning and inference.
Finding that difficult or crucial tokens get more iterations.

claims.claim: In a weight-tied ALBERT with per-token adaptive depth, tokens do not need the same number of iterations, and difficult or task-crucial tokens receive more.
claims.evidence_quote: We show that tokens do not require the same amount of iterations and that difficult or crucial tokens for the task are subject to more iterations.

claims.claim: Weight tying lets the encoder stack be read as one transformation iteratively applied, i.e. progressive refinement of token representations.
claims.evidence_quote: We interpret the repetition of this application as an iterative process where the token contextualized representations are progressively refined.

survey_notes: Abstract only (no arXiv id, no full text). Candidates record venue field: 'Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics' (DOI 10.18653/v1/2021.acl-srw.23, student research workshop). The halting mechanism and savings are not described in the abstract. Qualitative finding (harder tokens get more iterations) agrees with later token-level routing results such as MoR (2507.10524) and TaH (2511.08577).

title: BERT Loses Patience: Fast and Robust Inference with Early Exit
relevance_reason: Early exit by consensus of per-layer classifiers; main experiments use weight-shared ALBERT (a looped encoder), with BERT as a secondary untied backbone.
one_sentence: PABEE attaches a classifier to every layer and stops when t consecutive classifiers agree (patience); on weight-shared ALBERT it improves GLUE accuracy and speeds inference 1.57x, attributing gains to avoiding overthinking.
key_contributions: Patience-based exit: halt when internal predictions stay unchanged for t consecutive layers (a prediction-stability convergence rule).
Overthinking analysis: error rate rises after ~10 of 12 ALBERT layers while entropy keeps falling.
Simple theorem on when patience-based exit improves accuracy; robustness to adversarial attack.

setup.model_sizes: ALBERT-base (12M params, 12 layers), ALBERT-large (18M, 24 layers); BERT-base
setup.train_tokens_or_data: GLUE fine-tuning
setup.loops_train: all 12 (or 24) layers, internal classifiers trained with depth-weighted average loss
setup.loops_test: patience t (t = 6 in main comparison); exit when t classifiers agree
setup.baselines: ALBERT/BERT full, 6L and 9L variants, LayerDrop, head pruning, distillation (DistilBERT etc.), BranchyNet, Shallow-Deep
setup.benchmarks: GLUE; adversarial robustness on SNLI, MNLI, Yelp

claims.claim: Overthinking: on ALBERT-base the prediction entropy keeps decreasing with more layers while the actual error rate increases after 10 layers.
claims.evidence_quote: Although the model becomes more “confident” (lower entropy indicates higher confidence in BranchyNet [26]) with its prediction as more layers join, the actual error rate instead increases after 10 layers.

claims.claim: On ALBERT, patience-based exit improves accuracy over full-depth inference while speeding up inference 1.57x; on BERT accuracy is slightly lower than the original model.
claims.evidence_quote: approach consistently improves the performance of the original ALBERT model by a relatively large margin while speeding-up inference by 1.57×.

claims.claim: At the same speed-up ratio, PABEE beats confidence/entropy-threshold exits (BranchyNet, Shallow-Deep).
claims.evidence_quote: PABEE retains higher accuracy than BranchyNet and Shallow-Deep under the same speed-up ratio, showing its superiority over prediction score based methods.

claims.claim: Untied BERT benefits less, which the authors attribute to intermediate layers never having been connected to an output layer during pretraining (train/test mismatch for exits).
claims.evidence_quote: We suspect that this is because the intermediate layers of BERT have never been connected to an output layer during pretraining, which leads to a mismatch between pretraining and fine-tuning when adding the internal classifiers.

numbers.what: ALBERT-base and ALBERT-large with PABEE: speed-up and dev scores (MNLI, SST-2, STS-B)
Best patience for 12-layer ALBERT
numbers.quote: For a 12-layer ALBERT model, PABEE reaches peak performance with a patience of 6 or 7.

numbers.what: Extra parameters for internal classifiers
numbers.quote: Also, PABEE only introduces fewer than 40K parameters (0.33% of the original 12M parameters).

numbers.what: Speed-up range targeted for baselines
numbers.quote: ratio between 1.30× and 1.96× (the speed-up ratios of (AL)BERT-9L and -6L, respectively).

limitations: Classification/regression only (sequence-level exit); theorem assumes independent equal-accuracy classifiers, which the authors note is unrealistic; patience is a hand-set hyperparameter; how speed-up ratio is measured is not detailed in the main text.
venue: 34th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2020), Vancouver, Canada.
survey_notes: Earliest training-free-at-inference convergence rule in our set (prediction stability across consecutive depths) applied to a weight-tied encoder. Its overthinking observation (accuracy drops at full depth) predates and agrees with TaH (2511.08577) for looped LMs. PALBERT (2204.03276) reports that its learned PonderNet-style exit beats PABEE on most GLUE tasks and that PABEE does poorly on small datasets (CoLA, RTE); PABEE's own Table 1 shows gains over ALBERT. This disagreement involves re-implementation by PALBERT (it states all baselines were re-implemented). Deep supervision via depth-weighted losses on all exits.

title: Differentiable Adaptive Computation Time for Visual Reasoning
relevance_reason: Fully differentiable ACT replacement applied to the recurrent MAC reasoning cell (visual QA), not a looped transformer LM; relevant to halting objectives and exit rules.
one_sentence: DACT replaces ACT's non-differentiable halting with a monotone running mixture of step outputs trained with a ponder cost, plus an exact test-time halting rule when the top class can no longer be overtaken; on MAC/CLEVR it beats fixed-step MAC at equal average steps, unlike ACT.
key_contributions: Differentiable halting: each step outputs an answer and an uncertainty p_n; the final answer is a running monotone combination, so no hard cut during training.
Ponder-cost objective L + tau * rho(x) and an inference halting test that stops once remaining steps cannot change the argmax (same top-1 as full depth).
Shows ACT is insensitive to its ponder cost on MAC while DACT responds to it.

setup.train_tokens_or_data: CLEVR; GQA
setup.loops_train: MAC with max 12 steps (also 15), pre-trained 10 epochs without gating then fine-tuned with DACT
setup.loops_test: adaptive with halting test; max 12 or 15
setup.baselines: MAC with fixed steps (2, 3, 5, 9, 12, 15), gated MAC, MAC+ACT
setup.benchmarks: CLEVR accuracy vs average steps; GQA

claims.claim: At similar average computation, DACT-MAC substantially outperforms fixed-step MAC trained with the nearest integer number of steps.
claims.evidence_quote: models resulting from the application of DACT to MAC substantially outperform non-adaptive versions of MAC with similar computation cost in the CLEVR dataset

claims.claim: ACT does not respond to its ponder cost on MAC (a variant with zero ponder cost uses 3.2 steps), whereas DACT adapts computation to the penalty.
claims.evidence_quote: DACT responds as expected to variations in the ponder cost, adapting its computation accordingly, however, ACT proves to be insensitive to the ponder cost.

claims.claim: Raising the maximum to 15 steps hurts fixed gated MAC but helps DACT fine-tuned from 12-step models, giving the best accuracy (98.72%).
claims.evidence_quote: DACT-enabled-MACs with the maximum amount of steps set to 15 can be fine-tuned from existing 12 step models to obtain the best results of any model tested at 98.72% accuracy.

claims.claim: On GQA, where MAC gains little from more than two steps, adding adaptivity slightly reduces accuracy.
claims.evidence_quote: Accordingly, adding adaptability to the model does not increase accuracy but rather results in a small but measurable reduction in performance.

numbers.what: ACT with zero ponder cost: average steps and accuracy on CLEVR
numbers.quote: As an example, a variant of ACT without ponder cost (λ = 0.0) performs 3.2 steps on average and obtains an accuracy of 95.8%.

numbers.what: Best DACT accuracy on CLEVR (max 15 steps)
numbers.quote: can be fine-tuned from existing 12 step models to obtain the best results of any model tested at 98.72% accuracy.

numbers.what: Ponder cost giving accuracy comparable to best MAC
numbers.quote: DACT trained with a ponder cost of λ = 1 × 10−3 repeatedly obtains an accuracy comparable to the best achieved by any MAC and, on average, surpasses all tested alternatives.

limitations: Visual QA only; savings measured as average steps; on GQA the base model barely benefits from recurrence, so adaptivity slightly hurts; requires pretraining MAC without gating first.
survey_notes: Halting-objective lineage: shows ACT's ponder cost can be ineffective (computation insensitive to the penalty) and offers a differentiable alternative plus a provably output-preserving test-time exit rule (halt when the runner-up cannot catch up), which is a convergence-style rule computed from learned uncertainties. Two later looped-LM ideas appear here early: a soft mixture over all step outputs during training (cf. 2603.08391) and a safe exit test. Not a transformer. Sharing: MAC is described as a recurrent architecture; per-step weight tying is not stated explicitly in the text.

title: Comparing Fixed and Adaptive Computation Time for Recurrent Neural Networks
relevance_reason: RNN (not transformer) study comparing ACT's adaptive per-token repetitions with a fixed number of repetitions; a clean fixed-vs-adaptive loop-count ablation.
one_sentence: Repeat-RNN repeats each input token a fixed number of times rho (an ablation of ACT without adaptivity) and matches ACT on parity and addition, solving tasks in fewer SGD steps and sometimes with fewer repetitions.
key_contributions: Repeat-RNN baseline: constant rho state updates per token, returning the last state (vs ACT's halting-weighted average).
Shows on ACT's own tasks (parity, addition) that uniform extra computation matches ACT.
Reports that too many repetitions cause training instability.

setup.train_tokens_or_data: parity and addition tasks from Graves (2016)
setup.loops_train: Repeat-RNN rho in {2, 3, 5, 8}; ACT with ponder cost tau in {1e-1, 1e-2, 5e-3, 1e-3}
setup.loops_test: same as training
setup.baselines: plain RNN/LSTM, ACT-RNN/ACT-LSTM
setup.benchmarks: parity, addition (task solved at 98% accuracy)

claims.claim: A fixed number of repetitions per token matches ACT on the studied tasks, suggesting ACT's gains come mainly from extra computation rather than adaptivity.
claims.regime: iso_param; average repetitions reported for both
claims.evidence_quote: Surprisingly, such uniform distribution of the computational resources matches the performance of ACT in the studied tasks.

claims.claim: Repeat-RNN solves tasks with fewer training steps and fewer repetitions than ACT, but the right rho is task-dependent (rho = 2 fails on addition).
claims.evidence_quote: We observe that in our experiments (1) Repeat-RNN learns how to solve the tasks with less SGD training steps than ACT, and (2) it actually solves them with less repetitions than ACT.

claims.claim: Too many repetitions destabilize training on addition.
claims.evidence_quote: We see that when increasing ρ from 1 performance improves dramatically, but we also observe a limit: with too many repetitions the network shows instabilities with excessively long sequences.

Ponder-cost sensitivity is visible in its tables (ACT with the smallest tau fails on addition at 11.91 average repetitions; the largest tau collapses to ~1 repetition and fails). Supports the survey point that adaptive-depth papers must compare against a well-tuned fixed depth at matched average compute. Note: ACT applies repetitions per input token in an RNN, so 'depth' here is ponder steps between inputs.

title: Learning to Refine Hidden States for Reliable LLM Reasoning
relevance_reason: Iterates a small latent refinement module on final hidden states with an RL-trained depth controller; it does not loop the transformer layers.
one_sentence: ReLAR refines a pretrained LM's final hidden state for T steps before decoding, with T sampled from a categorical depth controller trained by actor-critic policy gradient on step-wise likelihood gain minus a fixed per-step cost.
key_contributions: Per-input depth controller over {0..Tmax} and an action controller for refinement direction, trained with policy gradient.
Dense step reward = log-likelihood gain of the target minus a fixed computation cost.

setup.model_sizes: LLaMA-1.1B, Gemma-2B, Qwen-3B backbones
setup.loops_train: T sampled from controller, up to Tmax
setup.loops_test: controller-selected T
setup.baselines: SFT-only, chain-of-thought and 7B general/medical LLMs
setup.benchmarks: medical (e.g. PubMedQA), math, multi-hop, open-ended generation

claims.claim: The refinement depth is chosen per input by an RL-trained controller whose reward is per-step likelihood improvement minus a fixed compute cost.
claims.evidence_quote: The controllers are trained with a policy-gradient objective based on step-wise likelihood improvement, enabling input-dependent reasoning control without relying on explicit reasoning.

claims.claim: Comparisons are to larger 7B baselines and the reward needs ground-truth targets, which the authors list as limitations.
claims.evidence_quote: First, our backbone models (LLaMA-1.1B, Gemma-2B, Qwen-3B) are smaller than the 7B baselines in our comparison, which may limit the direct comparability of results.

survey_notes: Adjacent example of RL-learned depth: a categorical depth policy trained with actor-critic on a dense likelihood-gain reward with explicit per-step cost c_d. The refinement operator is a separate module, not the transformer stack, so it is not a looped LM. Same 'likelihood gain' style of depth label as TaH2/RecurTrace in this group, but optimized by policy gradient instead of supervised imitation. Code location is given in text only as a GitHub handle path (tongyu0924/Learning-to-RefineHidden-States), not a full URL.

title: S-AI-Recursive: Convergent Recursive Reasoning
relevance_reason: Bio-inspired iterative controller evaluated in simulations and with task-specific recursive operators on Maze/Sudoku/ARC; not a looped neural language model.
one_sentence: Proposes a 'hormonal' convergence-plus-confidence stopping rule for iterative reasoning with warm-start memory; on Maze it cuts mean iterations from 20.00 to 11.31 at unchanged resolution, without comparison to trained looped models.
key_contributions: Multi-signal stopping criterion combining a convergence signal and a residual-uncertainty signal under an iteration budget.
Warm-start from stored 'engrams' that reduces stopping depth on recurring instances.

setup.loops_test: budget cap 20 iterations on Maze (fixed-depth reference)
setup.baselines: fixed-depth recurrence; residual-only stopping detector
setup.benchmarks: SAIUT+ simulations; Maze, Sudoku, ARC-style instances

claims.regime: n/a (same operator, fixed vs adaptive stopping)
claims.evidence_quote: On convergent Maze instances, adaptive hormonal stopping reduces mean depth from 20.00 to 11.31 iterations at unchanged resolution, a 43.4% reduction with paired Wilcoxon 𝑝 = 7.2 × 10−16.

numbers.what: Sudoku warm-start stopping depth

title: Radial Networks: Dynamic Layer Routing for High-Performance Large Language Models
relevance_reason: Proposes a token-level router that picks the next layer (allowing layer reuse), motivated by residual-ratio profiling of OPT/ViT; reuse is a design property, not an evaluated looped model.
one_sentence: Profiles residual-branch contributions in OPT and ViT (shrinking with model size), and proposes Radial Networks where an MLP router chooses the next layer per token, decoupling dynamic depth from layer count and permitting layer reuse.
key_contributions: Residual-ratio profiling: per-block contribution to the output falls as models grow (median 5% in OPT-66B).
Radial Network design: argmax MLP router over layers at each step, trainable by distillation or from scratch.

setup.model_sizes: profiling OPT-125M to OPT-66B, ViT up to 632M
setup.benchmarks: Wikitext2 profiling

claims.claim: Per-layer residual contributions are small and shrink with scale, suggesting per-token dynamic depth opportunities.
claims.evidence_quote: For example, the residual blocks in the OPT-66B model have a median contribution of 5% to its output.

relevance_reason: Weight-shared recurrent steps over a sentence graph (S-LSTM) with a per-word predicted number of steps; pre-Transformer-LM lineage of token-level depth assignment.

Depth embeddings so shared recurrent steps know the assigned depth.

setup.loops_train: per-word depth up to a maximum L
setup.loops_test: predicted per-word depth

Propagation penalty alpha controlling the step distribution; sensitivity study across datasets.

title: N-ODE Transformer: A Depth-Adaptive Variant of the Transformer Using Neural Ordinary Differential Equations
relevance_reason: Continuous-depth weight-shared Transformer block solved by an adaptive ODE solver, so the number of steps is set by solver error control; tested on PARITY.
one_sentence: Replaces residual layer updates with a neural ODE solved by adaptive Runge-Kutta so depth (time steps) is input-dependent; on PARITY the adaptivity does not overcome the Transformer's nonlocality limits, and arclength regularization does not help accuracy or efficiency.
key_contributions: N-ODE Transformer with solver-error-controlled step count as an implicit depth policy.
Negative result: adaptive depth from the solver does not fix PARITY; arclength penalty fails to improve accuracy or efficiency.

setup.train_tokens_or_data: PARITY binary strings
setup.loops_train: adaptive RK4 time steps
setup.loops_test: adaptive RK4 time steps
setup.baselines: vanilla Transformer with N layers
setup.benchmarks: PARITY

claims.claim: Solver-driven depth adaptivity does not remedy the Transformer's difficulty on PARITY, and penalizing trajectory arclength does not improve accuracy or efficiency.
claims.evidence_quote: We find, however, that the depth-adaptivity of the N-ODE Transformer does not provide a remedy for the inherently nonlocal nature of the parity problem, and provide explanations for why this is so.

Reports average test FLOPs (input-dependent) against unshared ResNets.

title: Layer Flexible Adaptive Computational Time
relevance_reason: ACT variant for RNNs where the number of stacked layers per time step is adaptive; RNN, not a looped Transformer.

claims.claim: Plain ACT with a single hidden vector gives only marginal benefits over basic RNN/seq2seq, motivating per-layer states.
claims.evidence_quote: Our experimental results show that ACT has marginal benefits over basic RNN or sequence to sequence (seq2seq) models, indicating that ACT, with a single hidden vector, cannot always work well.

numbers.quote: Experimental results show the performance improvement of 7% to 12% and indicate the model’s ability to dynamically change the number of layers along with the computational steps.

title: Learning to Reason With Adaptive Computation
relevance_reason: ACT over repeated inference-GRU attention steps for textual entailment; weight-shared step, not a looped LM.
one_sentence: Applies ACT to the number of attention-based inference steps in an SNLI model; adaptive steps give a small gain over a fixed-step model with a mean of 5 steps, but the ponder cost is hard to set.
key_contributions: First ACT-based multi-hop inference model for textual entailment.
Evidence that more fixed steps do not always help and that ponder cost tuning is fragile.

claims.claim: ACT's ponder cost is context dependent and difficult to set; optimal settings differed between encoder types.
claims.evidence_quote: Additionally, the Ponder Cost parameter shows context dependent behaviour – during preliminary experiments using RNN encoders, the optimal Ponder Cost settings were distinct.

claims.claim: The adaptive model uses a mean of 5 steps and is both cheaper and better than a large fixed number of steps.
claims.evidence_quote: our model takes a mean of 5 steps at inference time, meaning it is both more efficient and performant than using a large, fixed number of steps.

limitations: Could not replicate the original decomposable-attention baseline performance; SNLI construction may limit benefits of multi-step inference.
survey_notes: Historical: one of the earliest NLP reports that ACT's ponder cost is fragile and must be tuned per setting, a failure mode repeated in later halting papers in this group (2002.10306, 2604.21999).
